headline: How the Nvidia scandal has exposed a blind spot in US national security
html_content:
The fallout from the controversy surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and his alleged relationship with a Chinese business executive suspected of working for Beijing is spreading through Washington, raising questions about the Trump administration's handling of sensitive technology exports and putting Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's position under scrutiny.

Experts have warned that Washington's growing dependence on powerful technology executives could undermine US national security.

Senior White House officials are discussing whether Lutnick should be pushed out amid growing criticism of the administration's decision not to blacklist several Chinese companies and questions over its oversight of Nvidia's chip exports to China, Reuters reported.

Lawmakers from both parties have sought answers about how the Singapore-based company, Megaspeed International was able to continue accessing advanced Nvidia chips despite concerns that it could be helping Chinese clients circumvent US export restrictions.

Alice Huang, the woman Jensen had an affair with, and who is suspected of being a Chinese spy, worked as a senior executive at the company.

It has been alleged that Huang's relationship with Alice Huang helped facilitate at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip shipments to China.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reportedly confronted Lutnick last week over the Commerce Department's handling of Megaspeed, demanding to know why the United States had not already prohibited sales of advanced AI chips to the company, The New York Times reported.

The criticism comes amid a prolonged pause in the US government's efforts to expand its trade blacklist of Chinese companies.

The United States has not announced any additions to the list since October 2025, marking the longest gap between new postings in more than a decade.

Reuters reported earlier that the Commerce Department had held off adding China's AI startup DeepSeek, memory chipmaker CXMT and more than 100 other companies flagged as national security risks.

Concerns about escalating tensions between Washington and Beijing were among the reasons behind the delay.

Lutnick faces heat over Commerce dept's handling of Megaspeed

The scrutiny of Lutnick centres on the Commerce Department's handling of Megaspeed, suspected of helping Chinese technology firms obtain advanced Nvidia chips despite US restrictions.

Washington has restricted direct sales of advanced semiconductors to China since late 2022.

However, companies have sought to circumvent those restrictions by establishing data centres in Southeast Asia that can serve Chinese customers.

US officials have been investigating whether Megaspeed diverted Nvidia chips illegally into China, a charge the company has denied.

The New York Times reported in October 2025 that Commerce Department officials were investigating whether Megaspeed, which has close ties to Chinese technology companies, was helping Chinese firms bypass export restrictions through its purchases of Nvidia chips.

Despite those concerns, Nvidia continued selling chips to the company.

The possibility of adding Megaspeed to the US trade blacklist was subsequently discussed at a meeting involving deputies of cabinet officials.

However, Jeffrey Kessler, an under secretary at the Commerce Department, deferred the decision to Lutnick, according to the NYT.

Several Trump administration officials, including representatives of the State Department, later agreed that Megaspeed should be placed on the list.

The Commerce Department, which has final responsibility for issuing the relevant rules, did not act.

That inaction reportedly contributed to frustration across the administration and prompted Bessent's confrontation with Lutnick.

Bloomberg has also reported that Nvidia's general counsel intervened in a US government investigation into suspected chip smuggling involving Megaspeed.

Chris McGuire, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations who served in both the Trump and Biden administrations, described the handling of the matter as a "failure on multiple levels."

"The Department of Commerce has effectively outsourced export control enforcement to the private sector, which is favoring short-term business interests over long-term US national security," McGuire said.

"If the Department of Commerce is not willing to cut off organizations that are known to be working with Chinese intelligence services from the most advanced chips, it's not clear why it is bothering to administer any export controls at all," he added.

Trump faces questions over what he knew

While Lutnick is facing mounting pressure over the administration's export control policies, Trump has also been drawn into the controversy.

The New York Times reported that Trump was briefed about the intelligence concerning Huang's relationship with the woman while aboard Air Force One in May, shortly before the Nvidia CEO joined the president's trip to Beijing.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also serves as national security adviser, reportedly delivered the briefing.

It was at least the second time in seven months that Trump had been informed about intelligence concerning Huang's alleged involvement with the woman, the newspaper reported.

The account contradicts Trump's public assertion on Monday that he had not known about Huang's relationship when he travelled to China for a summit with President Xi Jinping.

"No, I didn't hear about it then," Trump said when asked whether he knew about the alleged relationship before the trip.

Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer criticised the president on Tuesday, saying reports that Trump had been briefed more than a year earlier raised serious questions about his handling of the matter.

"The press reports that Trump was briefed more than a year ago that Nvidia's CEO was having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, and Trump didn't do anything – anything – about it," Schumer said on the Senate floor.

"Can you believe that?" he added.

"What a dereliction of duty. He's supposed to protect America, not China, not his friends," Schumer said.

"Trump has been busy trying to defend Jensen Huang when he ought to be defending our national security. It's that simple, it's obvious."

Lawmakers demand answers from Lutnick and Huang

The political pressure is now growing on Capitol Hill, where lawmakers are seeking explanations from both the government and Nvidia.

Senator Tim Scott, a South Carolina Republican, sent letters on Thursday to Huang and Lutnick requesting that they testify before the Senate Banking Committee.

"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," Scott posted on X.

"The American people deserve answers," he added.

Republican Senator John Kennedy, meanwhile, declined to say whether Lutnick should lose his job when asked about the matter on CNN.

"I don't know yet," Kennedy said, adding that Lutnick needed to answer questions publicly and would be called to appear before Congress.

"This is as serious as an aneurism," he said.

Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren has also demanded accountability from the Commerce Department.

"Secretary Howard Lutnick and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China's military," Warren said.

Experts warn of growing influence of private sector on Washington

Beyond the questions surrounding individual officials, the controversy has exposed a broader dilemma in Washington's relationship with the technology industry: the growing influence of private-sector executives in areas that have become central to national security.

Julian Gewirtz, a senior research scholar at Columbia University's School of International and Public Affairs and a nonresident fellow at Harvard University's Belfer Center for Science and International Affairs, argued that the most troubling aspect of the episode may be the administration's response to warnings about Huang.

"Although the full Nvidia story is still emerging, the most alarming revelation may not be that Jensen Huang, America's most influential AI executive, was involved with a suspected Chinese spy. It may be that senior administration officials were warned about the danger and nevertheless continued relying on him to guide the United States' technological future," Gewirtz wrote in The Atlantic.

He said Washington's strategy had become unusually dependent on powerful private-sector actors whose commercial incentives could not automatically be assumed to align with national interests.

Cory Alpert, a researcher at the Lowy Institute and a PhD researcher at the University of Melbourne, similarly argued that the controversy exposed a contradiction in the government's relationship with Silicon Valley.

"Huang's affair shows a new contradiction at the heart of Washington's relationship to Silicon Valley. Private executives have more power than ever, while the institutions designed to protect America's national security haven't adapted to that change," Alpert wrote.

He argued that even when intelligence agencies identify potential security threats, political considerations can complicate the government's response.

Alpert said Trump could have moved against Huang but risked alienating an influential ally who has become central to America's technological competition with China.

Huang's embrace of the MAGA movement has also helped Trump cultivate political and economic support in Silicon Valley, he added.

"The decision to do nothing with the information developed by the FBI was a political one, made because Trump saw Huang as indispensable," Alpert wrote.

The emerging dispute therefore goes beyond Lutnick's future or the allegations surrounding Huang.

It raises questions about whether Washington can effectively enforce its technology restrictions when the companies and executives it relies on to maintain its global AI advantage also have substantial commercial interests in China.

For the Trump administration, the challenge is now to demonstrate that national security considerations will take precedence over those relationships, even as the political and economic stakes of the AI race continue to rise.

headline: SpaceX, Tesla could announce historic merger as soon as December: report
html_content:
Tesla and SpaceX could announce a historic merger as soon as December, according to a Bloomberg report published Thursday.

The potential merger could create what is projected to become the largest corporate deal on record.

The merger would combine Tesla’s electric vehicles, energy storage and robotics with SpaceX’s rockets, satellites and growing artificial intelligence operations.

SpaceX is valued at more than $1.9 trillion following its public listing, while Tesla is valued at about $1.5 trillion, pointing to a combined entity worth roughly $3.4 trillion to $3.5 trillion.

Musk moving quickly

According to the Bloomberg report, the possibility of an announcement in December comes from Elon Musk's "tendency to move quickly when it comes to corporate maneuvers."

Musk is the CEO of both Tesla and SpaceX. He is also the largest shareholder in both companies.

Boards and advisers for both companies are currently negotiating the terms of the tie-up, including the exchange ratio for Tesla shareholders and the governance structure of the combined entity.

An announcement could still slip into early 2027 if talks take longer, the report said.

Musk's 'good idea' in works

Musk has publicly endorsed the idea of a merger.

On SpaceX’s third-quarter earnings call in October, he said there was “a lot of merit to combining the companies” and termed the possibility to be “a good idea.”

He noted the boards had formed special committees of independent directors to evaluate the proposal and stressed that he could not participate in those discussions because he is a conflicted party.

Musk has highlighted synergies in artificial intelligence, including chip design, robotics, and orbital computing systems.

A previous Bloomberg report said that Musk was pushing to lock in the merger before President Donald Trump leaves office, aiming to announce a deal in the first half of 2027 so it could close during the current administration.

However, things have changed politically with Democrats gaining control of Congress in the midterm elections.

Musk was a key donor to the Republican Party and now faces a potentially less accommodating political environment for his businesses.

That timeline has now been accelerated if the latest report is to be believed.

Significant hurdles remain

Tesla’s operations in China present a major complication.

The country’s market accounts for roughly 20% of Tesla’s revenue and an even larger share of its earnings and free cash flow.

JPMorgan has identified Chinese regulatory approval as the single biggest obstacle to a deal, larger even than securing Tesla shareholder support.

Analyst Rajat Gupta noted that SpaceX’s extensive US government and defense contracts, combined with the fact that Starlink has never been approved to operate in China, create a potential conflict.

One possible workaround under discussion is to ring-fence Tesla’s China business, potentially transferring majority control to a Chinese consortium while allowing Tesla to continue generating revenue through licensing of its brand, Full Self-Driving technology and future products.

Any deal would still require regulatory clearances in multiple jurisdictions and approval from Tesla shareholders.

Former Tesla director Steve Westly explicitly named SEC approval among the hurdles. His broader concern points to a transaction in which Musk’s interests overlap across both sides of the negotiating table.

The special committees will need to demonstrate that their decisions reflect shareholders’ interests.

With the political environment changing, the merger could become tricky as scrutiny around Musk's businesses grows.

excerpt: Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 after meetings in a San Jose diner and quit as chief executive this week. Here is how a near-bankrupt graphics start-up became the company at the centre of the AI boom.
headline: Jensen Huang career timeline: from a Denny's booth to the centre of the AI boom
html_content:
Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia's chief executive ends a 33-year run in which he turned a graphics start-up, sketched out in a San Jose diner, into the company at the centre of the artificial intelligence boom.

Nvidia shares were at $170.34 in pre-market trading at 10:22 am GMT on Friday, up 2.5% from Thursday's close of $166.19.

At that close, the company was worth about $4 trillion, based on the 24.1 billion shares listed in its latest quarterly filing.

That is roughly $1.8 trillion less than at its record close of $239.24 on 6 October, Invezz calculations show, a 30.5% fall.

Huang told staff on 8 November that he had been unfaithful to his wife. The board accepted his resignation on 11 November, according to an 8-K filing, and chief financial officer Colette Kress is now interim chief executive, Nvidia said on Thursday. She presents third-quarter results on 17 November.

Our timeline of Huang's exit covers the past fortnight.

From a Denny's booth to a chip start-up

Huang was born in Taiwan in 1963 and sent to the US aged nine. He and his older brother were enrolled at the Oneida Baptist Institute in Kentucky before the family settled in Oregon.

As a teenager, he worked at Denny's, washing dishes and then clearing tables. "I washed the living daylights out of those dishes," he said in a 2024 Stanford Graduate School of Business interview.

He earned an electrical engineering degree from Oregon State University in 1984, designed microprocessors at AMD and then spent eight years at LSI Logic, while completing a master's at Stanford, Nvidia's 1999 IPO prospectus shows.

In April 1993, aged 30, he founded Nvidia with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, two Sun Microsystems engineers. The plan took shape over meetings at a Denny's in San Jose.

Near-collapse, then the first GPU

The first product nearly sank the company. The NV1, launched in May 1995, was built around Nvidia's own approach to 3D just as the industry settled on Microsoft's Direct3D, and sales slumped, the company's 1999 annual report says.

Nvidia abandoned a follow-up console chip for Sega and cut more than half of its staff. Sega turned its final payment into a $5 million investment that kept the start-up alive.

The episode gave Huang his best-known phrase. "The phrase '30 days from going out of business' I've used for 33 years," he told Joe Rogan in December 2025, according to Business Insider.

The RIVA 128, shipped in August 1997, turned things round. Revenue rose from $29.1 million in 1997 to $158.2 million in the year to January 1999.

Nvidia listed on Nasdaq on 22 January 1999, selling 3.5 million shares at $12 to raise $42 million. They closed the first day at $19.69, valuing the company at $626.1 million, The Wall Street Journal reported at the time.

That August, it launched the GeForce 256, which it marketed as the world's first GPU. Microsoft chose Nvidia graphics for the original Xbox, and in November 2001 Nvidia replaced Enron in the S&P 500.

The CUDA bet and the deep-learning breakthrough

The decision that would define Huang's legacy came in 2006, when Nvidia launched CUDA, software that let programmers use its graphics chips for general computing.

The payoff took years. In 2008, Nvidia took a charge for faulty laptop chips as the financial crisis hit, and its split-adjusted shares fell 85% from their October 2007 peak to a November 2008 low, Yahoo Finance data shows.

The turn came in 2012, when AlexNet, an image-recognition network trained on two Nvidia GeForce GTX 580 cards, won the ImageNet contest. Researchers began treating Nvidia GPUs as the default tool for deep learning.

In August 2016, Huang personally delivered Nvidia's first DGX-1 AI system to OpenAI, then a non-profit research lab.

He then pushed into data centre networking with the $6.9 billion purchase of Mellanox, completed in 2020. A $40 billion deal for Arm collapsed in February 2022 under regulatory opposition, and two crypto-mining booms left gaming sales swinging.

How data centres took over

The shift shows up in Nvidia's annual reports. In fiscal 2016, which ended in January 2016, data centre sales were $339 million, 7% of $5.0 billion in revenue, while gaming brought in $2.8 billion, the company's fiscal 2017 10-K shows.

Data centre overtook gaming in fiscal 2023, with $15.0 billion of $27.0 billion in sales. OpenAI had launched ChatGPT in November 2022, and demand for Nvidia's H100 chips surged.

In May 2023, Nvidia guided quarterly revenue of about $11 billion, well above Wall Street forecasts. The shares jumped 24% the next day, and the company first touched a $1 trillion valuation on 30 May.

Revenue then reached $60.9 billion in fiscal 2024, $130.5 billion in fiscal 2025 and $215.9 billion in fiscal 2026, its latest 10-K shows. Data centre sales were $193.7 billion of that, or almost 90%.

The momentum has continued into fiscal 2027 with the Blackwell and Vera Rubin platforms. Second-quarter revenue hit a record $96.2 billion, and Nvidia has guided $108 billion for the third quarter.

How Nvidia stock has grown since its IPO

Nvidia has split its stock six times: 2-for-1 in June 2000, September 2001 and April 2006, 3-for-2 in September 2007, 4-for-1 in July 2021 and 10-for-1 in June 2024. One IPO share is now 480 shares, so the $12 listing price works out at 2.5 cents.

At Thursday's close, that is a gain of about 6,650 times, before dividends, or roughly 37% a year, Invezz calculations show. A $1,000 stake at the IPO would now be 40,000 shares worth about $6.6 million.

The climb was far from smooth. The stock lost about 90% between January and October 2002, 56% in late 2018 after a crypto-driven inventory glut and 66% between November 2021 and October 2022.

Most of the value has come since ChatGPT. The shares are up almost 10 times from their close on 30 November 2022, the day it launched.

Nvidia was valued at $2 trillion in February 2024 and $3 trillion in June 2024. It became the first company to reach $4 trillion, in July 2025, and $5 trillion, on 29 October 2025, as Reuters reported at the time.

What Huang leaves behind

Huang built Nvidia around a single long bet, that the chips made for games could run the world's most demanding computing. That bet is now the business: a data centre franchise tied together by CUDA software, which has given Nvidia a lead that rivals are still trying to close.

He leaves without a named successor. The board has said it will consider internal and external candidates, and Kress keeps the CFO role while she runs the company.

Her first test comes on 17 November. Investors will be looking for the numbers, but also for signs that the company Huang built can keep its customers and engineers without him.

The board accepted his resignation on 11 November, according to an 8-K filing, and chief financial officer Colette Kress is now interim chief executive, Nvidia said on Thursday. She presents third-quarter results on 17 November. Our timeline of Huang's exit covers the past fortnight. From a Denny's booth to a chip start-up Huang was born in Taiwan in 1963 and sent to the US aged nine. He and his older brother were enrolled at the Oneida Baptist Institute in Kentucky before the family settled in Oregon. As a teenager, he worked at Denny's, washing dishes and then clearing tables. "I washed the living daylights out of those dishes," he said in a 2024 Stanford Graduate School of Business interview. He earned an electrical engineering degree from Oregon State University in 1984, designed microprocessors at AMD and then spent eight years at LSI Logic, while completing a master's at Stanford, Nvidia's 1999 IPO prospectus shows. In April 1993, aged 30, he founded Nvidia with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, two Sun Microsystems engineers. The plan took shape over meetings at a Denny's in San Jose. Jensen Huang's career, from Denny's to Nvidia's top job | Sources: Nvidia SEC filings, Nvidia, Fortune, Reuters, Invezz research Near-collapse, then the first GPU The first product nearly sank the company. The NV1, launched in May 1995, was built around Nvidia's own approach to 3D just as the industry settled on Microsoft's Direct3D, and sales slumped, the company's 1999 annual report says. Nvidia abandoned a follow-up console chip for Sega and cut more than half of its staff. Sega turned its final payment into a $5 million investment that kept the start-up alive. The episode gave Huang his best-known phrase. "The phrase '30 days from going out of business' I've used for 33 years," he told Joe Rogan in December 2025, according to Business Insider. The RIVA 128, shipped in August 1997, turned things round. Revenue rose from $29.1 million in 1997 to $158.2 million in the year to January 1999. Nvidia listed on Nasdaq on 22 January 1999, selling 3.5 million shares at $12 to raise $42 million. They closed the first day at $19.69, valuing the company at $626.1 million, The Wall Street Journal reported at the time. That August, it launched the GeForce 256, which it marketed as the world's first GPU. Microsoft chose Nvidia graphics for the original Xbox, and in November 2001 Nvidia replaced Enron in the S&P 500. The CUDA bet and the deep-learning breakthrough The decision that would define Huang's legacy came in 2006, when Nvidia launched CUDA, software that let programmers use its graphics chips for general computing. The payoff took years. In 2008, Nvidia took a charge for faulty laptop chips as the financial crisis hit, and its split-adjusted shares fell 85% from their October 2007 peak to a November 2008 low, Yahoo Finance data shows. The turn came in 2012, when AlexNet, an image-recognition network trained on two Nvidia GeForce GTX 580 cards, won the ImageNet contest. Researchers began treating Nvidia GPUs as the default tool for deep learning. In August 2016, Huang personally delivered Nvidia's first DGX-1 AI system to OpenAI, then a non-profit research lab. He then pushed into data centre networking with the $6.9 billion purchase of Mellanox, completed in 2020. A $40 billion deal for Arm collapsed in February 2022 under regulatory opposition, and two crypto-mining booms left gaming sales swinging. Nvidia annual revenue by market platform. Fiscal years end in late January | Source: Nvidia 10-K filings How data centres took over The shift shows up in Nvidia's annual reports. In fiscal 2016, which ended in January 2016, data centre sales were $339 million, 7% of $5.0 billion in revenue, while gaming brought in $2.8 billion, the company's fiscal 2017 10-K shows. Data centre overtook gaming in fiscal 2023, with $15.0 billion of $27.0 billion in sales. OpenAI had launched ChatGPT in November 2022, and demand for Nvidia's H100 chips surged. In May 2023, Nvidia guided quarterly revenue of about $11 billion, well above Wall Street forecasts. The shares jumped 24% the next day, and the company first touched a $1 trillion valuation on 30 May. Revenue then reached $60.9 billion in fiscal 2024, $130.5 billion in fiscal 2025 and $215.9 billion in fiscal 2026, its latest 10-K shows. Data centre sales were $193.7 billion of that, or almost 90%. The momentum has continued into fiscal 2027 with the Blackwell and Vera Rubin platforms. Second-quarter revenue hit a record $96.2 billion, and Nvidia has guided $108 billion for the third quarter. How Nvidia stock has grown since its IPO Nvidia has split its stock six times: 2-for-1 in June 2000, September 2001 and April 2006, 3-for-2 in September 2007, 4-for-1 in July 2021 and 10-for-1 in June 2024. One IPO share is now 480 shares, so the $12 listing price works out at 2.5 cents. At Thursday's close, that is a gain of about 6,650 times, before dividends, or roughly 37% a year, Invezz calculations show. A $1,000 stake at the IPO would now be 40,000 shares worth about $6.6 million. Nvidia share price since its 1999 listing, adjusted for six stock splits, log scale | Source: Yahoo Finance The climb was far from smooth. The stock lost about 90% between January and October 2002, 56% in late 2018 after a crypto-driven inventory glut and 66% between November 2021 and October 2022. Most of the value has come since ChatGPT. The shares are up almost 10 times from their close on 30 November 2022, the day it launched. Nvidia was valued at $2 trillion in February 2024 and $3 trillion in June 2024. It became the first company to reach $4 trillion, in July 2025, and $5 trillion, on 29 October 2025, as Reuters reported at the time. Nvidia's market value milestones. Values for October and November 2026 are Invezz calculations based on 24.1 billion shares | Sources: The Wall Street Journal, Reuters, Yahoo Finance, Nvidia SEC filings What Huang leaves behind Huang built Nvidia around a single long bet, that the chips made for games could run the world's most demanding computing. That bet is now the business: a data centre franchise tied together by CUDA software, which has given Nvidia a lead that rivals are still trying to close. He leaves without a named successor. The board has said it will consider internal and external candidates, and Kress keeps the CFO role while she runs the company. Her first test comes on 17 November. Investors will be looking for the numbers, but also for signs that the company Huang built can keep its customers and engineers without him. excerpt: Microsoft's Outlook and Exchange Online outage has run for almost 19 hours. Here is what Microsoft says broke, why its fixes have been slow to work, and how the disruption has hit traders, businesses and Microsoft stock.
headline: Why is Outlook down, and why can't Microsoft bring it back? What we know
html_content:
Microsoft's Outlook email service was still not working properly for many users on Friday morning, almost 19 hours after the outage began. Microsoft says its fixes are working only gradually and has given no time for full recovery.

The problems started at 16:17 GMT on Thursday, according to Microsoft's incident record for Exchange Online, the system behind business Outlook mailboxes. They spread from the Americas to Asia overnight and hit Europe as offices opened.

At 11:11 GMT on Friday, the Microsoft 365 Status account said recovery work had been completed on "portions" of the affected infrastructure. Mailbox access and delayed email were improving, it said, but some users could still see intermittent problems.

Microsoft has said it is not aware of any malicious activity behind the incident.

Which Microsoft services are down?

The outage is centred on Exchange Online. Microsoft said users might be unable to reach their mailboxes through Outlook on the web, desktop Outlook and mobile mail apps.

Any Microsoft 365 feature that relies on Exchange has also been hit. That includes calendar scheduling in Teams, parts of SharePoint and Copilot, and several security tools, according to Microsoft's advisory MO1550821. Features that do not depend on Exchange, such as joining Teams calls, have kept working.

Microsoft disclosed in April 2025 that it had more than 430 million paid Microsoft 365 commercial seats, which gives a sense of how many workers depend on the system.

Downdetector, which counts user reports, logged reports from 74 countries and territories within about an hour, NBC News reported. At the peak, there were 19,650 reports a minute across five Microsoft services, compared with fewer than 15 on a normal Thursday.

What Microsoft says went wrong

Microsoft has not published a root cause, promising a post-incident report once services are back. Its status updates, however, set out the problem in stages.

At 18:35 GMT on Thursday, it said part of its infrastructure was under "elevated load" in several regions. Less than an hour later, it clarified that the load was not caused by more traffic. Instead, a number of servers had become "unexpectedly unavailable", straining the ones left running.

Those servers were failing automated health checks and being pulled from service. Microsoft paused all deployments and began restarting machines.

By early Friday, Microsoft's admin centre updates said a process that sets up secure connections on the affected servers was becoming overwhelmed. Microsoft also said it had started reverting a recent network configuration change that "correlates with the start of impact".

That is not a confirmed cause: Microsoft had earlier said it had found no change linked to the start of the problem.

Why Microsoft has been unable to bring it back

The main difficulty, in Microsoft's own account, is that recovered servers did not stay recovered.

At 22:09 GMT on Thursday, Microsoft said its actions had "not provided the anticipated relief". Two hours later, it reported that servers it had returned to service could become unresponsive again as soon as they received traffic.

At 03:13 GMT on Friday, it said the changes applied had not taken effect as expected. A later update described a surge of calls from its routing systems to back-end servers after traffic was rebalanced, and machines stuck in a "bad state" that blocked a network change from syncing.

On Microsoft's account, each server that drops out pushes more work onto the rest. That is why engineers have been bringing capacity back slowly, limiting traffic in some places and draining, restarting and patching servers in stages.

The clearest progress came at about 07:24 GMT, when Microsoft said a patch to an "upstream authentication/routing configuration component" was improving server stability. It began extending the patch to regions entering business hours.

At 09:24 GMT, Microsoft reported "early stabilisation". It also extended its email timeout to 48 hours, so that messages stuck in queues are held rather than bounced back.

Outside experts have been struck by how long it has lasted. Gergely Orosz, a former engineer at Skype and Uber, told the BBC he "cannot recall" a business email outage taking this long to return to normal.

Markets, traders and public services hit

The disruption has spilled into financial markets. Bloomberg, in a report syndicated by The Straits Times, reported that traders were doing business by phone, WhatsApp and even fax, and that trade confirmations were backing up. In Singapore, some banks were unable to complete financing deals.

Euronext told listed companies to phone through corporate information because its listing teams could not receive emails, Reuters reported. Workhorse Group postponed its earnings release, and Richemont briefly delayed its half-year results, NBC News reported.

In the UK, NHS England said staff were turning to paper records where needed, The Guardian reported. Japan's government reported disruption to communications between ministries.

Microsoft shares were at $512.08 in pre-market trading at 11:19 GMT on Friday, according to Yahoo Finance data. That was 2.1% below Thursday's close of $523.00.

The stock had touched $529.66 on Thursday before the outage widened, and closed up 0.4%.

Amish Patel, head of equity research at Raymond James, told The Guardian the direct financial impact was "likely to be negligible". The bigger question, he said, is whether repeated outages make businesses rethink their reliance on one provider.

How it compares with other cloud outages

The outage is already longer than the two big cloud failures of October 2025.

Amazon Web Services' outage in its US-EAST-1 region ran for about 14.5 hours on 19-20 October 2025, according to AWS's own summary. Microsoft's Azure Front Door outage on 29-30 October 2025 lasted about eight and a half hours, from 15:41 GMT to 00:05 GMT, according to Microsoft's incident review.

The CrowdStrike incident of 19 July 2024 was different in kind. It was caused by a faulty security update that crashed about 8.5 million Windows computers, according to Microsoft, rather than by a failure in Microsoft's own cloud.

What happens next

Microsoft's focus is now on extending the fixes from Asia-Pacific to other regions and working through the backlog of delayed mail.

Its root-cause report, due after recovery, should show whether the network change was to blame and how Microsoft plans to prevent a repeat.

Until then, users may continue to see intermittent errors and late emails as service returns region by region.

headline: Wall Street futures mixed ahead of PPI data: 5 things to know before market opens
html_content:
US stock futures were mixed on Friday as investors awaited another inflation report following a volatile session marked by Nvidia's leadership shake-up and rising Treasury yields.

Dow Jones futures gained 0.19% and S&P 500 contracts added 0.13%, while Nasdaq 100 futures slipped 0.11%.

The cautious start followed Thursday's declines, when all three major benchmarks lost about 0.4%.

Microsoft's global service outage added to pressure on technology shares, while stronger earnings from Cisco and Applied Materials offered some reassurance about corporate investment.

5 things to know before Wall Street opens

1. Producer inflation puts Treasury yields back in focus

October's Producer Price Index is due at 8:30 am Eastern, with economists expecting headline prices to rise 0.4% and core prices 0.3%.

The release follows Tuesday's stronger-than-expected consumer inflation report, which reinforced expectations of another Federal Reserve rate increase.

The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield has climbed above 5.1%, making borrowing more expensive and pressuring equity valuations.

2.Microsoft outage raises questions about cloud reliability

Microsoft shares fell about 2.6% before the bell as disruptions affecting Outlook, Teams and Copilot continued into Friday.

The problems also affected Microsoft 365 integrations used by OpenAI and Anthropic, alongside government and business customers.

Microsoft reported signs of partial recovery but had not confirmed full restoration.

3. Nvidia faces its first full session under interim leadership

Nvidia shares recovered about 1.8% in pre-market trading after Thursday's 4.3% decline. The company confirmed Jensen Huang's resignation, appointing chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive while searching for a permanent replacement.

StoneX analyst Cody Acree downgraded Nvidia to Hold, arguing that leadership uncertainty justified greater caution over its valuation despite unchanged earnings estimates.

Investors are now looking towards Nvidia's 17 November results for reassurance about strategy, customer relationships and continued demand for AI processors.

4.Cisco and Applied Materials show investment remains resilient

Cisco reported quarterly revenue of $18.5 billion, up 24%, and adjusted earnings of $1.40 a share. It raised its annual outlook and expects $9 billion in AI infrastructure revenue from major cloud customers in fiscal 2027.

Applied Materials reported revenue of $10.41 billion, up 53%, with adjusted earnings of $4.16 a share. The chip-equipment maker also forecast approximately $11.1 billion in next-quarter sales.

5.Oil heads for another weekly loss despite supply threats

Brent crude traded around $96.04 a barrel at 07:41 GMT, while West Texas Intermediate stood near $88.59.

Both benchmarks were heading for a second consecutive weekly decline as President Donald Trump signalled that Washington could maintain its blockade of Iran without reaching a diplomatic agreement.

Attacks on tankers and Saudi energy facilities nevertheless kept supply risks elevated.

headline: Solana price faces a brutal death cross: could SOL crash below $70?
html_content:
Solana (SOL) extended its decline on Friday, falling 3.5% to trade around $80.54 as a broader cryptocurrency market sell-off pushed prices briefly below the psychological $80 level.

The cryptocurrency has lost 10% since the beginning of the week, adding to a prolonged correction that began after SOL traded above $120 in early October.

The latest decline coincided with Bitcoin's drop below $70,000, triggering widespread liquidations across the cryptocurrency derivatives market.

Crypto liquidations reach $1.64 billion as Bitcoin falls below $70,000

The cryptocurrency market experienced another wave of heavy selling on Friday, with Bitcoin's decline below $70,000 adding pressure to major altcoins.

According to CoinGlass, approximately $1.64 billion in leveraged cryptocurrency positions were liquidated over the past 24 hours.

Long positions accounted for $1.43 billion of the total, indicating that traders betting on higher prices suffered the largest losses.

The broader sell-off also coincided with weakness in technology stocks following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation amid scrutiny over personal relationships.

Bitcoin and several other cryptocurrencies have recently shown sensitivity to movements in artificial intelligence-related equities.

Solana's derivatives market continues to show signs of weakening demand as traders reduce their exposure to the cryptocurrency.

According to CoinGlass, SOL futures Open Interest is down 6.3% in the last 24 hours and now stands at $4.82 billion. 

Spot markets also experienced withdrawals, with reported outflows reaching $8.80 million.

The figures suggest that market participants are becoming increasingly cautious as Solana extends its decline.

Meanwhile, the SOL taker buy-to-sell ratio stands around 0.91, remaining below 1 since late July.

A reading below 1 indicates that selling activity is outweighing buying activity, suggesting that bearish traders retain an advantage.

Death Cross signals further downside risk for Solana

Solana's daily technical structure has deteriorated considerably following its decline from above $120 in early October.

At the time of writing on Friday, SOL trades around $80.54, significantly below its major moving averages.

The 50-day Exponential Moving Average (EMA) stands at $97.55, while the 200-day EMA is positioned near $98.62.

The 50-day EMA has crossed below the 200-day EMA, forming a bearish technical pattern known as a death cross.

This crossover typically reflects weakening medium-term price momentum relative to the longer-term trend.

Solana has also broken below a previously supportive ascending trendline, now positioned around $91.20.

The breakdown suggests that the cryptocurrency has lost an important technical structure that previously supported its recovery. The former trendline could now act as resistance if SOL attempts to rebound.

Momentum indicators also reinforce the bearish outlook. The daily Relative Strength Index (RSI) has fallen to approximately 21, placing Solana in deeply oversold territory.

An RSI reading below 30 generally indicates oversold conditions, while readings near 20 suggest that selling pressure has become particularly intense.

Meanwhile, the Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD) remains below zero, with its signal line around -0.81.

The negative reading suggests that bearish momentum continues to dominate, reinforcing concerns about further losses.

If the bearish trend persists, Solana's immediate downside support stands at $77.60.

This horizontal level represents an important area where buyers could attempt to stabilize the cryptocurrency after its recent decline.

With SOL trading around $80, the market is already approaching this support zone. A successful defense of $77.60 could allow the cryptocurrency to consolidate or attempt a temporary recovery.

However, a decisive breakdown below this level would weaken the technical outlook further. The next significant downside target stands at $67.50.

Despite the bearish outlook, Solana could attempt a recovery if buyers successfully defend the $77.60 support level.

The first significant resistance stands at $87.46. A sustained move above this level would suggest that short-term buying momentum is improving.

However, SOL would still face another important horizontal resistance around $95.82. Beyond this level, the 50-day EMA at $97.55 and the 200-day EMA at $98.62 form a concentrated resistance zone.

The proximity of these moving averages could make it difficult for buyers to sustain a recovery without stronger market demand.

A decisive breakout above the EMA cluster would improve Solana's technical outlook and suggest that the bearish momentum is beginning to weaken.

headline: Rolls-Royce share price rebound has stalled: is it a buy as it reaffirms guidance?
html_content:
Rolls-Royce share price has rebounded in the past few weeks, erasing some of the gains it made between August and October. RR jumped to a high of 1,393p, up by 20% from its lowest point in October. This article explores what to expect after the company published its financial results on Thursday.

Rolls-Royce Group reaffirmed, but did not raise its guidance

Rolls-Royce Holdings is the biggest industrial company in the UK, focusing on industries like civilian aircraft engine manufacturing, defense contracting, power, and the small modular reactor (SMR) industries. 

The company has benefited as all these businesses have thrived after the pandemic as the civil aviation industry has thrived. It is also benefiting from the ongoing boost in defense spending in countries in Europe, Middle East, and Asia.

Rolls-Royce Holdings published its trading statement on Thursday. The management reaffirmed its full-year guidance of between £4.7 billion and £4.9 billion of underlying profit and between £3.8 billion and £4 billion of free cash flow. Unlike in the past, the company did not raise its guidance. 

The management announced an interim share buyback of £1.5 billion, which will be completed when it publishes its full year results on February 25. This buyback is part of the existing plan of repurchasing shares worth between £7 billion and £9 billion, which will conclude in 2028.

In the statement, the management noted that its business was growing across the board, with it aircraft engine backlog being 2,500. It recently received large orders from companies like Avolon, Cathay Group, and Air China.

Most importantly, the company has seen the large engine flying hours grow by 4% in the first ten months of the year. This is crucial because the civil aviation industry went through major challenges as jet fuel prices soared and several large airlines slashed their trips. Indeed, the EFH from its Middle East airlines has moved above the pre-conflict levels. 

Rolls-Royce Holdings has also seen a strong demand in its defence business as countries continue boosting their spending. Most importantly, its power business is booming because of the ongoing artificial intelligence (AI) boom. Its order intake in this business jumped by 62%, bringing the total backlog to £8.6 billion. 

The company noted that orders for gas engines has more than tripled YoY, driven by data center demand. Also, it is now in the process of finalizing a major contract with a top hyperscaler. In a statement, the CEO said:

“Our transformation and the actions we are taking are creating a Rolls-Royce with a diversified portfolio of high-performing businesses, with greater resilience and significant growth potential.”

Rolls-Royce share price technical analysis

Rolls-Royce stock chart | Source: TradingView

The daily chart shows that the RR stock price has rebounded in the past few weeks. It jumped from a low of 1,158p on October 23rd to a high of 1,393p. The stock has now pulled back to the current 1,354p. 

It is consolidating along the 50-day Exponential Moving Average (EMA). The risk, however, is that it has formed a hanging man candlestick pattern, a common bearish reversal sign in technical analysis. 

The Average Directional Index (ADX) has dropped to 31.20 from this month’s high of 45, a sign that the recent recovery has started to fade.

Therefore, there is a likelihood that the stock will pull back further, potentially to the psychological level of 1,300p and then resume the uptrend. In the future, the stock will likely rebound, with the next important target being at 1,500p.

headline: Alice Huang held stakes in firms linked to banned Chinese tech giant Huawei: report
html_content:
Alice Huang, the businesswoman at the center of the controversy surrounding former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, held indirect stakes in Chinese companies linked to a data center that served Huawei, according to a CNBC report published Friday.

Huawei has been identified by Nvidia as one of its leading competitors in China, with Jensen Huang himself previously describing the company as highly competitive.

Huawei remains subject to US government restrictions over national security concerns.

How Alice Huang was linked to Huawei?

According to Chinese corporate records reviewed by intelligence firm Tesari and cited by CNBC, Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, became a co-owner of Shanghai Hexi, an investment firm focused on technology and data centers, as early as 2016.

In 2021, Hexi acquired a 27% stake in Shanghai Century Longteng, a data center developer.

Century Longteng, in turn, held a controlling 50.1% interest in Shenzhen Yifeng Technology, which operated a data center facility in mainland China.

The primary customer of that Shenzhen facility was Huawei Cloud, the cloud computing division of Huawei Technologies.

Hexi also provided guarantees for loans used to finance the facility, giving Alice Huang an indirect financial interest in infrastructure that supplied computing capacity to Huawei.

Hexi subsequently exited its stake in Century Longteng in 2024.

The period of Alice Huang's business involvement in the data center companies overlapped with the time when she and Jensen Huang were first publicly seen together, around December 2023.

US authorities suspect Alice Huang of acting on behalf of the Chinese government.

However, the CNBC report did not establish that the data center had obtained restricted Nvidia chips. It noted that a related company began purchasing Nvidia processors in 2023.

Moreover, in 2019, Alice Huang sold a cloud computing business called Osmanthus to Chinese gaming company 7Road.

A Singapore-based subsidiary of 7Road was subsequently renamed Megaspeed.

The company would later became a significant Nvidia partner in the region.

Megaspeed is under investigation over allegations that it was involved in the illegal transfer of restricted Nvidia chips to China.

Investigators are also examining possible links to Chinese intelligence operations. The company has repeatedly denied wrongdoing.

Huawei remains a major Nvidia competitor in China

The revelations also bring renewed attention to Huawei's growing position in China's artificial intelligence chip market.

Nvidia has identified Huawei as a leading competitor, particularly in artificial intelligence chips, graphics processors and related technologies.

In regulatory filings, Nvidia has listed Huawei among its key rivals in China, where the Chinese company has gained ground in the domestic AI chip market amid US export restrictions on advanced Nvidia products.

Huawei has faced extensive restrictions from Washington for several years over national security concerns.

The company was placed on the US Entity List in 2019, significantly limiting its access to American technology.

Earlier, The Information reported that Nvidia chips worth at least $7.5 billion had been delivered to Chinese firms through the relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang.

In 2022, the Federal Communications Commission also banned Huawei from selling telecommunications equipment in the United States, citing risks to data security and national communications infrastructure.

The latest revelations add another layer to the scrutiny surrounding Jensen Huang's reported personal relationship with Alice Huang.

The former Nvidia CEO has agreed to testify before Congress about the matter.

The session is expected to take place before Thanksgiving or in early December.

headline: AMD, Broadcom stocks fall 2% as Nvidia rebounds: is Wall Street switching sides?
html_content:
AMD and Broadcom stocks fell around 2% in Friday's pre-market trading, giving back part of Thursday's rally as investors tentatively returned to Nvidia following Jensen Huang's resignation.

Nvidia gained about 2.5% before the opening bell after falling 4.34% to $166.19 on Thursday. AMD had surged 5.86% to $585.30, while Broadcom climbed 5.54% to $364.36 in that session.

The reversal shows how quickly Wall Street is reassessing its bets on artificial intelligence chips.

Nvidia stock rebounds as investors reconsider Thursday's trade

The initial rush into AMD and Broadcom followed Huang's abrupt departure and the appointment of Nvidia finance chief Colette Kress as interim chief executive.

Investors questioned whether new management would preserve Huang's ambitious product strategy and close relationships with major customers.

That uncertainty made competing chipmakers attractive, particularly after Nvidia's sharp decline.

Friday's recovery may reflect bargain hunting, while the pullback in AMD and Broadcom could involve profit-taking after substantial gains earlier in the week.

“The market appears to be distinguishing between a problem for Nvidia and a problem for AI,” Pepperstone research head Chris Weston told ABC News on Thursday.

His distinction matters, as companies can redirect investment towards alternative chip suppliers without abandoning plans for data centres or AI applications.

Equally, buying shares in an Nvidia competitor takes seconds. Changing an established computing platform can involve lengthy technical testing, software changes and contract negotiations.

AMD and Broadcom still have powerful growth drivers

AMD challenges Nvidia more directly through its Instinct AI accelerators and server processors. Its third-quarter revenue rose 45% to $13.4 billion, while Data Center sales jumped 97% to a record $8.5 billion.

William Blair analyst Sebastien Naji upgraded AMD to Outperform on Thursday, according to TipRanks.

He cited Nvidia's leadership uncertainty, Intel's supply problems and improving prospects for AMD's next generation of AI systems.

Broadcom has a different business model. It supplies custom accelerators and networking technology to cloud operators developing their own computing infrastructure.

Its fiscal third-quarter AI semiconductor revenue reached $16.7 billion, up 221% from a year earlier. Management expects that figure to reach approximately $21.7 billion in the following quarter.

Ming-Chi Kuo of TF International Securities said Google's custom-chip ecosystem could “win more trust from customers and the supply chain”, according to Investing.com. Broadcom is a key partner in that ecosystem.

Nvidia's earnings will test the recovery

Nvidia retains advantages that competitors cannot easily replicate, including its CUDA software ecosystem, advanced processors and deep customer relationships.

Its latest quarterly revenue reached $96.2 billion, with Data Center contributing $89 billion. Existing infrastructure commitments are unlikely to vanish simply because the company is changing chief executives.

That is important because Nvidia's software tools and hardware designs remain embedded in major customers' systems and spending plans.

“We still have little evidence of a pause in the AI buildout,” Morningstar analyst Brian Colello wrote on Friday. Nonetheless, he lowered his Nvidia fair value estimate from $310 to $250, citing greater uncertainty about future products and leadership.

That mixture of resilient demand and heightened risk helps explain the week's volatile trading.

Nvidia is scheduled to report fiscal third-quarter earnings on 17 November, having previously forecast revenue of approximately $108 billion.

Investors will scrutinise margins, customer spending and management's guidance under Kress.

headline: Why is Bitcoin down today? BTC crashes below $68,000 amid mass liquidations
html_content:
Bitcoin fell below $70,000 on Friday for the first time since August as forced selling in leveraged trades intensified a decline driven by US inflation fears and withdrawals from exchange-traded funds.

The cryptocurrency traded at $69,227 at 11:53 GMT, down 5% from the same time on Thursday, according to Yahoo Finance data. It earlier touched about $67,627 before recovering some ground.

Ethereum also slipped below $2,000, while Solana and XRP weakened. Bitcoin was heading for a sixth consecutive weekly loss, showing how quickly confidence has faded since its October 2025 peak.

Why Bitcoin price is falling today?

The fall accelerated when Bitcoin breached $70,000, a level where traders had accumulated leveraged bets on rising prices.

CoinGlass figures showed $1.47 billion in cryptocurrency positions liquidated over 24 hours early Friday. Bullish positions accounted for $1.31 billion, making forced long selling the dominant source of pressure.

A separate CoinDesk snapshot put Bitcoin-specific liquidations at roughly $677 million. The totals reflect different observation times, not additional losses to be added together.

Sean McNulty, a derivatives trader at AQC Tech, explained in comments published by Bloomberg that crossing $70,000 triggered automatic closures of heavily leveraged positions, accelerating the decline.

When exchanges close losing positions to recover borrowed funds, selling can spread even without fresh negative news. Thin order books magnify that effect.

Inflation and ETF withdrawals deepen the pressure

Tuesday's US inflation figures added to the strain. Headline consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, while core prices climbed 0.3%, both above forecasts.

The stronger reading reinforced expectations of a Federal Reserve interest-rate increase in December, supporting the dollar and reducing appetite for speculative assets.

Rich Rosenblum, co-founder of crypto market maker GSR, told Bloomberg that a firmer dollar and turbulence in artificial intelligence stocks had hit bullish Bitcoin trades. Nvidia's management upheaval added to broader unease.

Institutional flows have also weakened. US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $643.6 million in net withdrawals this week through Thursday, as per SoSoValue data. Year-to-date net flows have turned negative by $1.56 billion.

Those redemptions complicate a rebound because new buyers must absorb ordinary selling alongside continued fund withdrawals.

Can Bitcoin defend $67,500 before the Fed's next test?

The area around $67,500 is now a near-term reference after Friday's low. Bitcoin also briefly slipped beneath its 200-week moving average near $68,000, a widely watched longer-term trend gauge.

Keith Alan, co-founder of Material Indicators, warned in analysis reported by Cointelegraph that a further deterioration in weekly momentum could bring much lower levels into view.

A move back above $70,000 could ease immediate pressure; a sustained fall below $67,500 would instead expose the $65,000 area.

Traders await Friday's US producer-price report and December's Fed decision. MSCI's scheduled removal of Strategy from its indexes on 30 November is another potential source of volatility.

Readers exploring how to buy Bitcoin or comparing the best crypto exchanges should distinguish ordinary spot purchases from leveraged trading, where losses can accelerate rapidly.

headline: Cerebras stock jumps 13% as AI chipmaker raises annual forecast, signs Microsoft deal
html_content:
Cerebras Systems shares CBRS surged nearly 13% in premarket trading on Friday after the AI chipmaker raised its annual revenue forecast, reported a surprise profit and announced Microsoft as a new customer, signalling growing momentum in its challenge to Nvidia's dominance of the AI computing market.

The rally could add nearly $4 billion to Cerebras' market value if the gains hold, offering investors some reassurance amid concerns about the sustainability of massive AI infrastructure spending.

The company's latest results also come as the AI sector faces heightened uncertainty following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation amid controversies surrounding his personal life.

Cerebras raises revenue outlook after strong third quarter

Cerebras now expects full-year core revenue of between $940 million and $960 million, up from its previous guidance of $880 million to $890 million.

It also raised its core gross margin forecast by one percentage point to a range of 42% to 44%.

Analysts polled by FactSet had expected full-year core revenue of $887.5 million and a gross margin of 42%.

The company reported adjusted earnings of 12 cents per share for the third quarter, compared with analysts' expectations of a loss of 14 cents.

Core revenue came in at $230.9 million, beating estimates of $214.7 million.

Revenue increased 70% from $135.7 million a year earlier, although growth slowed from 103% in the second quarter.

Cerebras, which sells both AI chips and cloud computing capacity, also expects revenue to triple in 2027, reflecting continued demand for computing power used to run AI models.

“The demand for fast inference, which is what we specialize in, is enormous,” Chief Executive Andrew Feldman said in an interview, referring to the process of AI models generating outputs.

“The business is cooking with gas,” he added.

Microsoft deal adds to Cerebras' customer base

The company said on Thursday that Microsoft had signed a deal to become a new customer, adding to its existing partnerships with Oracle and OpenAI.

Financial terms of the agreement were not disclosed.

However, Feldman said Microsoft signed the deal in October and that revenue contributions were expected to begin in the first quarter of 2027.

“We believe revenue begins to show up in Q1 ’27,” Feldman said in an interview with CNBC.

The agreement represents another step in Cerebras' efforts to expand its customer base as technology companies compete to secure computing capacity for increasingly demanding AI workloads.

Analyst price targets reflect contrasting views

Despite the strong results, analysts have offered mixed assessments of Cerebras' valuation and growth prospects.

Needham lowered its price target to $200 from $300 while maintaining a Buy rating, citing multiple compression across the AI sector.

Its revised target is based on an enterprise value of approximately eight times its calendar 2028 revenue estimate.

Mizuho also cut its target to $240 from $300, while retaining an Outperform rating.

Wedbush took a more positive view, raising its price target to $205 following the company's third-quarter performance and upbeat fourth-quarter outlook.

Morgan Stanley reiterated its Overweight rating and $178 price target, pointing to improved gross margins and stronger fourth-quarter revenue guidance driven by hardware shipments.

Despite Friday's potential gains, Cerebras shares remained under pressure following their market debut.

As of Thursday's close, the stock was down 47.2% from its May IPO price of $185 per share.

excerpt: El Niño is already here and could become the strongest on record this winter. Here is what it is, when it will peak, why forecasters and the IMF are worried, and what it could mean for crops, food prices and markets.
headline: What is El Niño and why is the world so worried? Impact on crops and markets
html_content:
The tropical Pacific is in the grip of one of the strongest El Niño events on record, and the world’s weather agencies say it has not yet peaked.

On Thursday, the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) said a strong-to-very strong El Niño is likely through January–March 2027, with a better than 79% chance.

Sea temperatures in the key monitoring zone were 2.5°C above average in October, its Climate Prediction Center said.

NOAA also puts the odds of a “historic event”, stronger than any El Niño since 1950, at about 60% for this winter.

That matters far beyond the Pacific, because El Niño shifts rain belts around the globe.

What is El Niño?

El Niño is the warm phase of a natural climate cycle known as the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, or ENSO.

Normally, trade winds blow from east to west across the equatorial Pacific, piling warm water up near Indonesia, where it fuels heavy rain. Off South America, cold, nutrient-rich water rises to the surface.

During El Niño, those winds weaken or even reverse. The warm water spreads east, the rain belt follows it, and the cold upwelling off Peru is suppressed.

NOAA declares El Niño when sea temperatures in the Niño 3.4 region of the central-east Pacific stay at least 0.5°C above average for several months in a row. La Niña is the mirror image, with readings at least 0.5°C below average.

Since February, NOAA has used a relative index, RONI, which strips out the general warming of the tropical oceans so events can be compared fairly.

When is El Niño coming, and how strong will it be?

It is already here. NOAA declared El Niño on 11 June.

The event has strengthened steadily. NOAA’s relative index reached +1.97°C for August–October, just behind the +2.07°C recorded at the same stage of the 1997 event. The highest three-month reading in its records is +2.40°C, from December 1982 to February 1983.

On the traditional index, the August–October reading of +2.46°C is already the highest for that season since 1950.

NOAA’s median forecast has the relative index peaking at about +2.53°C in November–January, which would beat that 1983 record, before the event weakens in early 2027.

Australia’s Bureau of Meteorology said on 10 November that all the models it assesses have the warming peaking in November or December, with El Niño levels lasting into the southern hemisphere autumn.

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said in September there was a near-100% chance of El Niño lasting through February 2027, the first time one of its updates had been so unequivocal.

NOAA’s probabilities show El Niño fading to a 38% chance by April–June, when neutral conditions become the most likely outcome.

Why is the world so worried?

The first worry is heat, as El Niño releases ocean heat into an atmosphere already warmed by human activity.

The EU’s Copernicus climate service said on 11 November that October 2026 was the warmest October on record, at 1.75°C above pre-industrial levels. It said 2026 is virtually certain to be only the second calendar year above 1.5°C, after 2024.

The biggest temperature effect usually comes the following year. Climate site Carbon Brief projects 2027 at about 1.7°C above pre-industrial levels, with a 96% chance of being the warmest year on record.

The second worry is cost. A 2023 study in Science by Dartmouth researchers Christopher Callahan and Justin Mankin estimated global income losses of $4.1 trillion and $5.7 trillion in the five years after the 1982–83 and 1997–98 El Niños.

The third is food. IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva told AFP in October that the fund was preparing to support vulnerable countries.

“We are concerned about food security,” she said, also citing pressure on inflation from food prices.

What impact could it have around the world?

El Niño tends to bring drought to India, Southeast Asia, eastern Australia, southern Africa and northern South America. It usually brings heavier rain to the southern US, coastal Peru and Ecuador, and southern Brazil, Uruguay and northern Argentina.

Much of that is already happening. India’s June–September monsoon delivered 87% of its long-period average, the fourth-lowest since 2001, the India Meteorological Department said.

Southern Africa’s regional climate forum expects below-normal rain across much of the region through March, a risk for maize, the staple crop.

In Central America, many subsistence farmers lost more than 75% of their first maize and bean harvests, the EU’s Joint Research Centre said on 10 November.

Peru cancelled its second anchovy season of 2026 in October after warm water pushed fish deeper. The country supplies up to 20% of the world’s fishmeal and fish oil, SeafoodSource reported.

Not everywhere is suffering. Australia’s ABARES forecasts a 29.9 million-tonne wheat crop, 3% above the 10-year average, while Argentina and southern Brazil should gain from wetter weather.

What is the likely impact on agriculture and food prices?

The FAO Sugar Price Index rose 6.6% in October to its highest level since December 2024, the UN agency said on 6 November, citing problems in Brazil, India and Thailand. Raw sugar futures for March delivery traded at 18.39 cents a lb at 12:26 GMT on Friday, 27% higher than a year ago.

FAO expects world rice production to fall 2.5% to 552 million tonnes, the first drop in four seasons, partly because of El Niño. US rough rice futures settled at $18.29 per hundredweight on Thursday, about 50% above their level on 11 June.

Policy can amplify the weather: in July 2023, as the last El Niño developed, India banned exports of non-basmati white rice.

Ivory Coast’s weather agency has warned that El Niño could cut the country’s 2026–27 cocoa harvest by 21% to 25%, Reuters reported on 11 November. New York cocoa futures were at $5,257 a tonne at 12:27 GMT on Friday, up about 42% since El Niño was declared.

The Indonesian Palm Oil Association (GAPKI) estimates El Niño could cut Indonesia’s output by up to 3 million tonnes, mostly in 2027. Malaysian palm oil futures closed at 4,462 ringgit ($1,093) a tonne on Friday, up 4.79% this week.

What does El Niño mean for markets?

For investors, the main channel is inflation. Morgan Stanley Research said in August that El Niño has historically had little bearing on global asset prices outside commodities, but that a “super” event could break that pattern.

It named sugar as the crop most likely to see a price boost and flagged copper supply risks in Chile and Zambia. It said food-driven inflation could delay rate cuts in Brazil, Colombia and Peru, and that emerging-market sovereign debt was among the most exposed assets.

Sugar producers and suppliers of seeds and fertiliser could benefit, the bank said, while companies that buy those crops could face higher costs.

What happens next?

NOAA’s next update, due on 10 December, should show whether the event has set a new record.

Even after the Pacific cools, the effects will linger. Palm oil losses, southern Africa’s harvest and the expected heat of 2027 suggest El Niño will shape commodity markets well into next year.

headline: Palo Alto Networks stock rises as KeyBanc upgrades shares to Overweight
html_content:
Palo Alto Networks shares surged 3% in premarket trading on Friday after KeyBanc Capital Markets upgraded the cybersecurity company, citing expectations of stronger security spending and its position in the market for artificial intelligence protection.

KeyBanc raised its rating on Palo Alto Networks (PANW) to Overweight from Sector Weight and assigned a price target of $380.

The upgrade comes ahead of the company's fiscal first-quarter earnings report, scheduled for November 18.

The new target implies approximately 18% upside potential from Thursday's closing price.

The upgrade follows a roughly 20% decline in Palo Alto Networks shares over the past month.

KeyBanc said the pullback, alongside positive checks on the company's first-quarter performance, had created an attractive entry point.

KeyBanc sees stronger cybersecurity spending through 2027

KeyBanc analyst Eric Heath said the firm expects security budgets to accelerate through 2027, which could benefit Palo Alto Networks.

In a note to clients, Heath said the company was well positioned to benefit from the trend towards consolidation in cybersecurity, supported by its product offerings in areas including AI security.

He also pointed to the growing need for businesses to defend against threats associated with the accelerating adoption of artificial intelligence.

Heath said Palo Alto Networks was executing better than many of its cybersecurity peers, adding that the firm's positive first-quarter checks supported the decision to upgrade the stock.

The analyst also highlighted the recent share-price decline as a factor behind the improved investment opportunity.

Investors await Palo Alto Networks' quarterly results

Investors will now focus on Palo Alto Networks' fiscal first-quarter results, due on November 18, for further indications of demand across its cybersecurity business.

Analysts expect the company to report earnings of $0.97 per share on revenue of $3.31 billion, according to consensus estimates cited by Seeking Alpha.

The results could provide further insight into the company's ability to benefit from increased security spending and demand for solutions that protect businesses as they adopt AI technologies.

Palo Alto Networks provides network, cloud, and security operations solutions.

The company serves more than 80,000 enterprise customers worldwide, including over 75% of the Global 2000.

Its position across several areas of cybersecurity has also attracted attention from market commentators.

CNBC's Jim Cramer recently expressed confidence in Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike Holdings, saying he preferred the two companies over Netskope, another cloud security platform.

Cybersecurity stocks remain in focus

The KeyBanc upgrade comes as investors assess which cybersecurity companies are best positioned to benefit from changing enterprise security requirements.

The increasing use of AI creates opportunities for security providers, while also introducing new threats that businesses need to address.

KeyBanc's outlook rests partly on the expectation that companies will increase their security budgets through 2027 and that Palo Alto Networks will continue to execute ahead of many of its peers.

However, investors will be looking for confirmation of these trends in the company's upcoming results.

The November 18 earnings report will therefore be an important near-term event for the stock, as investors assess revenue performance, earnings, and management's outlook against expectations for stronger cybersecurity spending.

headline: Nvidia shares edge up on Friday: is the worst over?
html_content:
Nvidia NVDA shares edged higher in premarket trading on Friday, recovering slightly after a sharp selloff tied to the abrupt resignation of longtime CEO Jensen Huang.

The stock was up 2% ahead of the opening bell after closing Thursday at $166.19, down 4.3%.

That followed deeper losses earlier in the week as the leadership crisis intensified.

Trading has been volatile, with the stock hitting lows near $149 in the previous session before recovering.

Investors have been rattled by uncertainty over succession and the broader implications for Nvidia's dominant position in artificial intelligence chips.

Colette Kress, the company's former finance chief, has taken over as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent replacement.

The premarket bounce suggests some dip-buying after the heavy selling, although shares remain well below recent highs.

The broader market was also in green in futures trading, with technology stocks continuing to reflect caution around the AI sector.

Opinions divided over Nvidia's short-term recovery

Wall Street analysts have responded with caution, with several warning that the leadership turmoil could weigh on the stock even as Nvidia's underlying business remains strong.

"Nvida's competitive advantage and customers don't disappear overnight," Seth Hickle, chief investment officer at Mindset Wealth Management, told Reuters.

"The market is trying to determine whether this is a temporary leadership crisis or something that fundamentally changes the AI investment thesis."

Hickle said implied volatility would likely remain elevated until Nvidia's earnings report and subsequent conference call provide more clarity about the company's plans following the leadership change.

Lior Prosor, managing partner at deep-tech venture capital and private equity fund Deep33, also expects continued uncertainty in the near term.

"In the short term, we expect the market to remain jittery. Investors will want clarity on permanent leadership and several quarters of evidence that NVIDIA continues to execute against its roadmap and delivery expectations," Prosor told Yahoo Finance.

"Until then, even if the stock looks increasingly cheap on fundamentals, it may take time before buying that discount becomes an easy trade."

Ryan Zurrer, founder and director of investment firm Dialectic, sees the selloff differently and considers the lower valuation an opportunity.

"You're buying this thing at 10 times forward-looking earnings for a company that, for all intents and purposes, seems irreplicable in the global AI infrastructure base," Zurrer was quoted as saying by Yahoo Finance.

Analysts downgrade Nvidia

Several analysts have either downgraded Nvidia shares or reduced their price targets following the latest developments.

Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon cut his price target from $400 and downgraded the stock from Market Outperform.

However, he maintained that the company's underlying business remained strong despite the leadership turmoil.

"Fundamentals of the business (if not the leadership) are clearly still intact with numbers that remain massive (and probably still headed higher). We don’t think the company should have huge issues operating while engaged in a search for new leadership. And (of course) the shares are almost absurdly cheap (and getting cheaper as we speak); clearly there is a lot of bad news getting priced in here," he said.

He nevertheless cautioned against making a large investment in the stock at this stage.

"On the other hand, we find it hard to advocate stepping in here in size as there will no doubt be more allegations to come," he said.

headline: US wholesale inflation rises less than expected in October
html_content:
US wholesale prices increased less than expected in October, offering some relief on the inflation front, although a sharp acceleration in annual producer prices and persistent cost pressures could complicate the Federal Reserve's next interest rate decision.

The producer price index (PPI), which measures the prices domestic producers receive for goods and services before they reach consumers, rose a seasonally adjusted 0.3% during the month, below the 0.4% increase expected by economists surveyed by Dow Jones, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on Friday.

Core PPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, also increased 0.3%, in line with expectations.

However, the annual headline PPI rate accelerated to 6.5%, up 0.2 percentage points from the previous reading and marking its highest level since November 2022.

Goods prices drive annual producer inflation higher

The details of the report showed that inflationary pressures remained broad across several parts of the economy.

Prices for final demand goods increased 0.5% in October, although more than 60% of the advance came from goods excluding food and energy.

Prices in the latter category actually declined 0.1% during the month.

On an annual basis, the goods index jumped 10.2%, marking its biggest 12-month increase since October 2022.

Final demand services prices rose 0.2%, with much of the increase linked to transportation and warehousing services.

Truck transportation of freight recorded a 3.9% increase.

Meanwhile, prices for intermediate processed goods surged 14.6% from October 2025, the largest annual increase since July 2022.

Intermediate services prices climbed 6.9%, their biggest gain since November 2022.

A measure of producer prices that excludes food, energy and trade services increased 0.5% during October, pointing to continued cost pressures beyond volatile commodity markets.

Persistent inflation complicates Fed's December decision

The report comes ahead of the Federal Reserve's next policy meeting on December 8-9, with policymakers facing mounting questions over how to balance inflation risks against the broader economic outlook.

Earlier this week, the BLS reported that consumer inflation was hotter than expected in October.

Headline and core consumer prices both increased 0.4% and 0.3%, respectively, exceeding forecasts by 0.1 percentage point.

The latest readings suggest that inflation remains some distance from the Fed's 2% target.

Markets have been pricing in a rate hike at the Federal Reserve's December 9 meeting as almost certain, with traders assigning a 100% probability to an increase, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.

The odds of a 25-basis-point hike stand at 89.7%, while the probability of a larger 50-basis-point increase is 10.3%.

Policymakers are also concerned that higher fuel prices linked to the Iran war and President Donald Trump's tariffs could be spreading through the economy.

While the Fed might ordinarily look through temporary supply-driven price increases, their broadening impact could indicate that inflation is becoming more entrenched.

Stock futures extended their gains following the PPI release, while Treasury yields were mixed as investors assessed the implications for monetary policy.
