headline: Why the AI trade is hard to kill, but easy to frighten
html_content:
The artificial intelligence investment boom has developed a familiar pattern: a new threat emerges, technology stocks sell off, and investors soon begin buying the dip.

DeepSeek’s arrival in January 2025 challenged assumptions about the cost of developing advanced AI.

Nvidia fell nearly 17% in a day, losing about $593 billion in market value, before recovering around 8% the next session.

During the tariff turmoil in April 2025, the Nasdaq-100 suffered its fourth-worst two-day loss since 2007, before recording its second-best single-day gain over the same period on April 9, after the White House announced a 90-day pause in reciprocal tariffs.

More recently, the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5% on November 5 as investors worried that Democratic victories in the US midterm elections could slow data-centre construction.

The index rebounded 2.7% on November 9, although falling oil prices also helped lift broader markets.

The rebounds have not erased all losses.

But the sequence captures the trade’s central tension: investors believe AI could transform businesses while questioning the valuations and financing behind it.

Why does the AI trade keep coming back?

For Louisa Loran, an executive adviser and global business strategist who previously worked at Google, the answer begins with demand.

“The AI investment boom has faced several existential threats, but none of them has touched what investors are actually betting on, which is use,” she said.

DeepSeek’s low-cost models raised concerns that cheaper systems could undermine the economics of US AI developers and reduce demand for high-end chips.

Loran argues that lower costs could instead encourage wider adoption.

“DeepSeek made AI cheaper, and lower access cost has always increased uptake in an industry, so it strengthened the case for adoption rather than weakening it,” she said.

Adoption, however, is not yet translating consistently into corporate profits.

A McKinsey survey published in August 2026 found that 80% of respondents said AI had improved individual productivity, while 37% reported at least some contribution to their organisation’s earnings before interest and taxes.

Loran said she had seen this lag while working with Google customers.

“Infrastructure scales at the speed of capital, while returns arrive at the speed at which organisations change how they work and make decisions,” she told Invezz.

Companies may build infrastructure before redesigning processes and training staff to capture its benefits.

Harry Hamann, founder of investment research firm InvestWealth, offered a financial explanation.

He said the market scares had not broken the revenue and cash-flow engines funding the largest technology companies.

The biggest spenders, he argued, have financed much of the build-out from existing businesses, allowing infrastructure orders to continue despite falling share prices.

Hamann separates short-term market movements from longer-term fundamentals.

“Over days, it is mostly positioning: crowded holdings, leverage and options hedging turn a headline into a 5% to 15% move. Over quarters, fundamentals decide, which is why every dip so far has been bought,” he told Invezz.

While Hamann’s framing relies on broad market mechanics rather than a quantitative decomposition of each pullback, it highlights a key divide between short-term trading and long-term capital allocation.

Why are trillion-dollar companies swinging so violently?

The dollar sums involved can make moves appear unprecedented.

A 5% decline in a company valued at $5 trillion erases $250 billion in market value.

But market capitalisation is the share price multiplied by all outstanding shares; a fall in that figure does not mean an equivalent amount of cash has left the stock.

The percentage moves still matter. Franklin Templeton Institute estimated that hyperscalers and AI-adjacent companies together made up nearly 46% of the S&P 500’s market value as of September 30, 2026.

The figure includes companies supplying or adopting AI, not just businesses that sell AI products.

That concentration means a change in sentiment towards AI can affect a significant share of the broader market.

It can also magnify crowded trades, momentum strategies and leveraged positions.

The Bank of England’s July 2026 Financial Stability Report said high concentration, correlated momentum-driven positions and increased leverage could amplify a fall in AI-related share prices if investors reassessed the sector’s earnings prospects.

Options-market data provide a clearer picture of how investor positioning changed as technology stocks came under pressure.

In a November 2 analysis, Cboe Global Markets found that the proportion of stocks among the S&P's top 100 showing inverted call skew — a sign of unusually bullish options sentiment — had fallen from 44% in early October to 10%.

At the same time, retail put buying in mega-cap technology stocks on Cboe's exchanges reached a year-to-date high, accounting for 34% of retail opening trades, compared with an average of 24%.

The figures suggested that investors were moving away from bullish bets on further gains and increasingly seeking protection against potential declines.

That shift became more pronounced during the November 5 sell-off.

In a follow-up analysis published on November 9, Cboe found that increases in S&P 500 put skew and put convexity accounted for 5.5 points of the 11.5-point increase in the VIX that day.

Yet the rise in hedging demand did not translate into widespread expectations of a broader market sell-off.

Cboe's COR1M implied correlation index reached just 22% on November 5, compared with a historical average of around 70% on days when the S&P 500 fell 4% in a session over the previous two decades.

Five of the 11 S&P 500 sectors also finished the week higher.

Cboe said the options market was still pricing a rotation out of AI and technology stocks rather than a broader market contagion.

The data point to a sharp change in investor positioning and demand for downside protection, but do not establish that options trading caused the underlying share-price declines.

These mechanics help explain why a headline can produce a larger move than the immediate change in earnings outlook.

Still, explaining the market mechanics behind violent swings does not prove that underlying valuations are safe from fundamental shocks.

On November 12, Nvidia shares tumbled as much as 14.3% intraday following CEO Jensen Huang’s sudden resignation amid an internal conduct and security probe.

Yet the stock recovered to close down just 4.3% after CFO Colette Kress was named interim CEO—while rival chipmakers AMD and Broadcom surged roughly 6% on the day.

That intraday reversal underscored how quickly governance uncertainty can be repriced in a central AI stock without breaking broader appetite for the sector's hardware."

Nor are large percentage declines in major indices unprecedented. The Nasdaq Composite fell 12.3% on March 16, 2020, during the Covid-19 market shock.

What makes today’s moves striking is the enormous market value attached to a concentrated group of AI-linked companies, not proof that markets have entered an entirely new category of volatility.

When does volatility become dangerous?

A share-price fall is not automatically a financial-stability event.

The risk grows if an AI repricing undermines debt used to finance data centres and chips, or spreads losses to lenders.

Professor Iwa Salami, professor of financial law and regulation at the University of East London, said both business concerns and investor behaviour contribute to volatility.

Worries about profits can trigger selling, while crowded ownership, borrowing and rapid efforts to reduce risk can intensify declines and affect the wider market.

Salami said a more serious warning would be companies spending heavily on AI for years without generating sufficient returns.

"Falling profits, mounting debt or a lasting drop in AI investment would be more worrying than a short-term fall in share prices. Regulators should also watch whether losses spread to banks and other financial institutions," the professor told Invezz.

That concern is reflected in official assessments.

A survey of 20 market contacts included in the Federal Reserve's May 2026 Financial Stability Report identified concerns about AI-related equity valuations and capital expenditure increasingly funded by debt.

The report clarified that these responses reflected the views of survey participants, not those of the Federal Reserve Board or the New York Fed.

The Bank of England said AI-related companies' use of credit markets had accelerated rapidly, spanning public markets, private credit, leveraged finance and structured finance.

It described the pace of investment as historically unprecedented, although it found little evidence so far that AI financing was crowding out other borrowers.

It warned that declining hyperscaler free cash flow and increasingly complex financing arrangements could create risks if earnings disappoint or refinancing conditions worsen.

The Bank for International Settlements said financial-stability risks from the AI boom appeared moderate, but warned that its sustainability hinged on companies meeting high earnings expectations.

It also noted that equity prices had moved considerably ahead of debt-market valuations.

The AI trade has so far survived shocks to assumptions about model costs, trade policy and political support for infrastructure.

But resilience should not be confused with immunity.

AI may become more widely used even if some companies have overbuilt, borrowed too heavily or paid too much for infrastructure.

The technology can succeed while particular investments fail.

For investors, the question is whether companies financing AI’s expansion can earn returns that justify the capital committed.

For regulators, it is whether the debt links built around it could transmit a correction into the wider economy.

The next scare may pass, as previous ones have. The test will be whether the cash flows and financing behind the build-out remain intact.

headline: Is AI Mode killing the internet’s search-based business model?
html_content:
When AI chatbots burst onto the scene, there was chatter that they would kill Google search and the surrounding business models. 

The latest fiscal results are shedding some light on this prediction, and it seems that it is indeed affecting publishers and companies depending on Google search traffic. 

Google, in a bid to stay ahead of chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude, launched its own AI mode. 

However, that is creating another problem, as more users use AI mode instead of visiting the websites providing the information. 

There was a simple business model. Google crawled and indexed websites and displayed those links to users and directed traffic towards publishers. 

Those visits provided advertising revenue, attracted subscribers for higher-value information and allowed websites to build audiences. 

Artificial intelligence is challenging this model. 

Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode provide users with information directly on search-result pages, reducing the need to click through to individual websites. 

The consequences are beginning to appear in company earnings.

Reddit reported a sharp decline in search referrals.

Freelance platform Fiverr also highlighted the impact of AI-related disruption on traditional search engine optimisation (SEO) work. 

Google is also facing challenges in generating advertising revenue from AI mode compared to revenue from conventional search.

The development raises a broader question about the sustainability of the open internet. 

If websites lose the traffic that finances their content, what happens to the information that AI models themselves depend on?

Industry executives believe the shift could represent a lasting change in the economics of the internet, with implications for publishers, companies and users. 

Google’s AI transformation is changing the economics of search

Google started AI Mode as an answer to ChatGPT.

ChatGPT’s introduction made companies question whether conversational AI would eventually replace a search engine.

The initiatives appear to be generating greater engagement. 

Google reported its highest query growth in five years. 

However, increased search activity does not necessarily translate into higher traffic for websites or greater advertising revenue for Google.

Alphabet’s third-quarter results highlighted this. 

The company reported search growth of 12%, down from 19% at the beginning of the year, while search and advertising revenue fell short of Wall Street expectations.

Google also warned of further pressure on search-revenue growth in the fourth quarter.

Another indication of the changing economics is the deceleration in paid-click growth. 

Google’s paid clicks increased 13% year over year in the first quarter, but the growth rate slowed to 8% in the third quarter.

AI Mode could be contributing to this shift.

Unlike conventional search, where users typically encounter several links and advertisements before visiting a website, AI Mode attempts to provide a more comprehensive response within Google's own interface.

This creates a different user experience. Consumers can ask follow-up questions, compare information, and explore topics without necessarily leaving Google.

For the search giant, the challenge is converting that engagement into revenue. 

For publishers, the problem is users tend to stay with Google’s AI Mode and end up not visiting their sites. 

Philipp Schindler, Google's chief business officer, acknowledged during the company's earnings call that AI Mode currently generates lower monetisation than traditional search, despite recording more queries.

Google is attempting to address the issue by expanding advertisements in AI Mode to additional countries and experimenting with new advertising placements as conversations progress.

Reddit's traffic decline offers an early warning

The consequences of this changing relationship are becoming particularly visible among websites that have historically depended on Google for audience acquisition.

Reddit is one of the clearest examples.

The platform's shares plunged approximately 29% on October 30 after its third-quarter results and outlook disappointed investors.

Investors were particularly concerned about weaker-than-expected user growth and the deterioration in search referrals.

Reddit CEO Steve Huffman said search traffic had declined by more than one million referrals per week during October.

He also warned that daily active users coming from search could decline by more than 10% in the fourth quarter.

Huffman suggested that Google's AI Overviews were becoming a more prominent part of the search experience, pushing traditional website links further down the results page.

“What started as a feature is now the full search experience,” he said during the earnings call. “And, at a minimum, it pushes everyone down the search page. And then, on top of that, the experiences themselves are not traffic drivers.”

He added that users continued to want Reddit's content, but Google was no longer directing visitors to the platform at the same rate.

"Google is crawling us as hard as ever, so the demand hasn't changed from their point of view either. The reality is, the AI mode does not drive traffic, not for us and not to anybody," Huffman said on the post-earnings call.

The distinction is important because Reddit's business model benefits from user engagement, conversations, and the extensive archive of discussions available on its platform.

Historically, Google helped introduce new users to those discussions. 

AI-generated answers can now provide information extracted from similar conversations without requiring users to visit Reddit.

The platform is responding by tightening access to its content. 

Reddit said it would begin trialling a requirement for users to log in to access the website in international markets before the end of the year.

The move is intended partly to restrict AI bots from scraping its content.

Publishers face a weakening incentive to produce free content

The problem extends beyond Reddit.

Fiverr CEO Micha Kaufman described the changes as an earthquake across the internet, arguing that organic clicks were declining as more consumers turned to AI assistants to find information.

“The internet as we’ve known it for the past 20-plus years is going away, and it’s going to completely change,” Kaufman said. “It’s dying.”

Fiverr's third-quarter revenue declined 15.8% from the year-earlier period.

In its shareholder letter, the company highlighted the impact of AI-related disruption on traditional SEO services, saying the changes had affected both low-value and high-end work on its platform.

The development could have broader consequences for digital publishing.

Many online businesses depend on organic search traffic to attract readers and generate advertising impressions. 

Others use search referrals to acquire customers, promote subscriptions or direct visitors towards commercial products.

When AI-generated summaries answer questions directly, fewer users may reach the original websites.

Monica Tartau, Head of Marketing at Aurora Labs, believes this represents a structural rather than temporary change.

“It looks more permanent than temporary to me,” Tartau told Invezz.

She argued that the traditional relationship between Google and publishers is changing because the search engine increasingly answers questions itself rather than directing users to the websites providing the underlying information.

Expert view

Google used to send people to websites. Now it answers the question itself (AI Mode & AI Overview) and keeps them there. It still needs the web for material, but it doesn’t need to send users to it the same way.

Head of Marketing at Aurora Labs
Monica Tartau

According to Tartau, this weakens the financial incentive for websites to continue producing freely accessible information.

“A lot of sites made money or justified the work because people clicked through from Google,” she said.

The expert added that when AI mode provides the answer before the user clicks, “that page view, ad, signup, or sale often doesn’t happen.”

The problem is particularly relevant for businesses that rely on large volumes of relatively inexpensive content and organic search traffic.

AI search could undermine the information it depends on

The potential consequences extend beyond the immediate financial pressure on publishers.

AI search engines rely on information produced across the internet. 

News organisations, specialist publications, research platforms and independent websites contribute material that helps AI systems answer questions.

If those publishers lose the revenue that finances their work, the supply of original information could deteriorate.

Michael Heinrich, CEO of 0G, described this as one of the more serious long-term risks associated with AI-powered search.

“Producing original information costs money,” Heinrich told Invezz.

Expert view

Whether you're running a newsroom, conducting scientific research or publishing specialist industry analysis, someone has to fund the work. If AI systems consume that information while reducing the audience publishers can monetize, eventually the economics stop making sense for some of them

CEO of 0G
Michael Heinrich

. 

Heinrich expects publishers to respond in different ways. 

“Larger publishers can negotiate licensing agreements, specialist platforms may move behind paywalls, and smaller independent sites could simply publish less,” the expert noted.

That creates a potential feedback loop.

“The problem for AI companies is that they still need a steady supply of accurate, current information. If fewer people are producing original material, AI systems risk drawing from an increasingly repetitive pool of secondary content, including material generated by other AI systems.”

This creates a contradiction for the AI industry. 

The technology could become increasingly effective at extracting and presenting information while simultaneously weakening the financial incentives that encourage people to produce that information in the first place.

Can Google make AI Mode as profitable as traditional search?

If Google backs AI Mode, it needs to find a way to transfer the advertising economics from search to AI Mode. 

In traditional search, a user searching for a particular product or a service can see sponsored links alongside organic results. 

Advertisers can compete for those placements, while Google earns revenue from commercial interactions.

AI Mode offers a different opportunity.

Because users can provide more context and ask follow-up questions, the platform may gain a better understanding of their needs and purchasing intentions.

Heinrich believes this could eventually create new advertising opportunities.

“If a user asks an AI assistant to compare laptops for a particular budget, for example, there's a very clear commercial intent that advertisers would be willing to pay to reach,” he said.

Google has already begun expanding advertisements within AI Mode, including to additional countries and through experiments involving advertisements that appear as conversations continue.

However, integrating advertising into AI-generated answers introduces another challenge: maintaining user trust.

In conventional search, sponsored links are generally distinguishable from organic results. 

Within a conversational AI response, the distinction between an objective recommendation and a paid placement could become less obvious.

Heinrich expects advertising decisions to continue reflecting user intent, relevance, conversion potential and advertiser bids.

But he cautioned that commercial incentives should not determine what an AI system presents as factual information.

If consumers begin questioning whether recommendations are genuinely useful or simply favour advertisers, Google could undermine the credibility of the product it is trying to monetise.

Tartau also noted that Google is already expanding advertisements in AI Mode, but said the company has acknowledged that these placements currently generate less revenue than conventional search advertisements.

She said Google's expectation is that users conducting early-stage research may become more commercially valuable as they continue asking follow-up questions.

For now, however, the ability to generate more interactions has not necessarily translated into equivalent monetisation.

Are paywalls and login requirements a good solution?

As search traffic becomes less reliable, websites are likely to reconsider how they distribute their content.

One option is restricting access through subscriptions, registration requirements, or other forms of login barriers.

Reddit is already planning this. By limiting access, the platform will make it more difficult for AI systems to scrape its discussions. 

Tartau said that for Reddit, “a login stops some of that, gives them a direct relationship with users, and more control.”

However, login requirements are not necessarily an effective solution for every publisher.

Tartau said such restrictions could also prevent casual visitors from discovering a website through search.

For Reddit, the strategy may make sense because its value lies partly in its extensive archive of conversations and user-generated discussions.

For a conventional publisher, the calculation is different.

“But if your business depends heavily on people discovering you through Google, putting everything behind a login can be quite damaging. You're effectively asking people to commit to your platform before they've had an opportunity to understand its value”, Heinrich added.

Experts expect many websites to adopt a middle-ground approach.

Michael Heinrich said there would be a hybrid approach where “publishers keep enough content publicly accessible to attract new readers while protecting premium research, proprietary data or specialist analysis.”

He believes publishers with differentiated content and established audiences could have greater opportunities to negotiate licensing agreements with AI companies.

However, smaller websites that depend heavily on search discovery could face greater difficulties.

The expert also highlighted an important distinction: restricting access through a login wall does not automatically establish ownership rights or prevent every form of AI use.

He added that a publisher's negotiating position will depend on the uniqueness of its information, licensing arrangements and the technical controls used to enforce access.

“Most sites will probably do something in the middle: leave some stuff open so they can still be found, put the better material or tools behind a login, and try to build more direct relationships through newsletters and apps so they’re less dependent on Google,” Monica Tartau added. 

The internet's next business model remains uncertain

Despite the hybrid model’s possibility, there is still uncertainty for the publishers. 

Funding the content that populates the internet is always a challenge. Free information was supported by advertisements driven through clicks. 

As AI models eat up advertisements and clicks, it threatens to close off the internet and make users pay for basic access. 

Key takeaway

The open web only works if someone is still willing to fund the content that lives on it.

Head of Marketing at Aurora Labs
Monica Tartau

The internet's search-based business model is therefore facing more than a decline in clicks. 

It is confronting a fundamental question about who gets paid when information is created, indexed, extracted, and delivered through artificial intelligence.

headline: Cricket's billion-dollar goldmine: why IPL works and can it rival NFL, NBA, MLB?
html_content:
Most Americans would know, or correctly guess, that football, or soccer, as they call it, is the most-followed sport in the world.

But ask which sport comes second, and there is a good chance their guesses will be wildly off the mark.

In fact, outside the Indian subcontinent and some other Commonwealth countries, many people would struggle to guess the correct answer.

It is cricket, a bat-and-ball game that attracts enormous audiences across densely populated South Asian countries and several other parts of the world.

The India-Pakistan match at the 2019 Cricket World Cup in England attracted an estimated 1 billion viewers worldwide.

That popularity has gradually been transformed into a commercial powerhouse through the Indian Premier League, or IPL, one of the world's biggest sporting leagues that many people outside cricket-playing nations may never have heard of.

How big is the IPL?

There is little that comes close to the Super Bowl in the United States when it comes to sporting events and television audiences.

Nielsen data shows that 125.6 million viewers tuned in to watch the 2026 Super Bowl, in which the Seattle Seahawks defeated the New England Patriots to lift the trophy after 12 years.

Now consider this: an average IPL league match this year attracted 277 million viewers. The final had an even bigger audience of 400 million, according to the official broadcaster.

On a per-match basis, few other sporting leagues come close to the viewership numbers generated by the IPL.

And those eyeballs translate into serious money.

A recent Sportico report valued the Mumbai Indians, the joint most successful IPL franchise, at $2.1 billion.

That puts the team in a valuation league comparable to Major League Baseball's Detroit Tigers and the NHL's Vancouver Canucks, both considered mid-tier franchises in their respective competitions.

Sportico's analysis put the average IPL franchise valuation at $1.7 billion, with almost every one of the 10 teams worth at least as much as some of the lowest-valued franchises in the NHL and MLB.

And the IPL has not even completed two decades of existence.

The four major American leagues have all decorated histories stretching way back into the 20th century.

How did the IPL become so big?

The IPL began in 2008 with the aim of tapping cricket's largely untapped commercial potential.

Eight franchises, some partly owned by hugely popular Bollywood stars, participated in the inaugural edition.

Today, 10 city-based franchises compete in the tournament, with reports of further expansion continuing to circulate.

Every team plays 14 league games, with four top teams advancing to the playoffs.

A total of 74 games are played in a season, far lower than major leagues in America and even Europe.

A strict salary cap is put in place to ensure all teams are on a level playing field.

The cricket-mad Indian public embraced the format, and the league has since grown into a giant in the global sporting business.

The financial transformation has been remarkable. The original eight teams averaged $90 million in value. Sportico's latest calculations put the average franchise valuation at $1.7 billion.

That value is not just theoretical. Recent franchise sales have attracted interest from major global sports investors, including Manchester United owners, American billionaire families, and private equity giants.

Royal Challengers Bengaluru was acquired by a consortium including Blackstone and Bolt Ventures for $1.78 billion ahead of this season.

Another franchise, Rajasthan Royals, was acquired for $1.61 billion by a group that includes Lakshmi Mittal and his family, which also owns a stake in the Boston Celtics.

So what makes these franchises so attractive to investors?

"IPL teams benefit from extreme scarcity with only 10 teams, cost certainty ensuring every team is profitable and potential opportunity in a massive market with a young demographic," Kurt Badenhausen, co-author of the Sportico report, told Invezz.

The combination of a limited number of franchises, a massive potential audience and predictable league economics gives investors exposure to a market that is difficult to replicate.

The money behind the cricket

The financial foundation of the IPL is its lucrative broadcast and sponsorship model.

The Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) sold the league's media rights for ₹48,390 crore, approximately $6.2 billion at the time of the auction, for the 2023-2027 cycle.

That agreement made the IPL the world's second-most valuable sports league on a per-match basis, trailing only the NFL.

But how does that money reach individual franchises?

Venkat Ananth, a longtime sports journalist who runs State of Play, a publication focused on the business of Indian sport, explained that the IPL operates through a central revenue-sharing arrangement.

The BCCI sells media rights to broadcasters and sponsorship rights to commercial partners, then distributes approximately 45%-50% of the proceeds to the teams.

This central pool is critical to franchise economics. Ananth estimates that media-related income accounts for roughly 70% of a team's revenue, while the remaining 30% comes from non-media sources such as ticketing, merchandise and local sponsorships.

For investors, Ananth identifies two major attractions: "One, it is a validation of the Indian consumption story. Two, because of the league's dynamics," he tells Invezz.

The IPL is a closed league, with no promotion or relegation, and has a limited number of franchises. That scarcity, combined with the enormous media rights opportunity and the profile of its owners, makes the teams particularly attractive assets, he said.

The league's growth numbers reinforce that appeal.

The IPL has recorded a compounded annual growth rate of 17.73%, exceeding the growth of all four major American sports leagues as well as the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite over the same period.

Sportico's analysis also puts the average IPL franchise revenue multiple at 22.9, the highest among major sporting leagues.

A revenue multiple measures how much a business is valued at relative to the revenue it generates.

In this case, a 22.9-times multiple means the average IPL franchise valuation is equivalent to 22.9 times its annual revenue. Put another way, investors are valuing each $1 of franchise revenue at approximately $22.90.

It is a measure of how much investors are willing to pay for a business relative to its current sales, rather than its profits.

A high multiple can reflect expectations of future growth, but it also means valuations depend heavily on the ability of franchises to sustain and expand their commercial earnings.

A lucrative broadcast deal forms the backbone of what IPL founder Lalit Modi has described as a "recession proof" model.

However, there are questions about whether the next broadcast rights agreement can sustain the league's extraordinary growth.

Can the IPL boom be sustained?

During the last rights cycle, Viacom18, backed by India's second-richest man Mukesh Ambani, and Disney India competed extensively to secure the broadcasting rights, pushing up the value of the deal.

However, the two entities merged in 2024 to form a new broadcaster, JioStar.

The merger created a major player in India's sports broadcasting market, raising questions about whether the next rights auction, due in 2027, will attract the same level of competition and generate an equally lucrative deal.

Ananth believes the next cycle could be challenging, but he also sees an opportunity for franchises to diversify their businesses.

"Yes next rights cycle could be a tricky one but it could also be a blessing in disguise," he said.

Historically, franchises have relied heavily on the central media revenue pool, leaving less incentive to develop other commercial opportunities. Ananth believes that could now change.

"There is a lack of incentive to push the boundaries in terms of going beyond media rights. That is changing, gradually, and with a flat media rights cycle and sponsorship categories such as Real Money Gaming also being vapourised overnight, the hope is that most teams will start taking this bucket seriously."

One example worth watching is the recent partnership between the Mumbai Indians and Nike.

The two signed a multi-year agreement, making Nike the franchise's official kit partner. It marks Nike's first official kit deal with an IPL franchise since supplying the now defunct Deccan Chargers in 2008.

For Ananth, such partnerships reflect how teams are beginning to look beyond broadcasting revenue and develop themselves as consumer-facing businesses.

He believes more franchises are starting to think of themselves as consumer product companies, a shift he considers important for the league's next stage of growth.

The opportunity, he said, is to build something more enduring than media and sponsorship income alone. Teams could develop merchandise, brand partnerships and other commercial products that allow them to recover some of the value potentially lost through a flatter media rights cycle.

But that requires franchises to rethink the experience they offer supporters.

"Teams need to think of it as an experience. Every franchise must own the experience," Ananth said.

That includes everything from the team's visual identity and merchandise design to making products affordable for fans. It also means ensuring that attending an IPL match feels worth the money, with stadium facilities and the overall match-day experience becoming central to the business.

In other words, franchises must become more than teams that play cricket for two months every year. They need to build brands that supporters want to engage with throughout the year.

Can the IPL compete with America's biggest sports leagues?

So can the IPL continue pushing its limits and eventually compete with the biggest American sporting leagues?

Ananth believes the potential exists.

"The conditions are very much there. The television product is good. The gameplay is good," he said.

To become as big as these NFL or MLB or NBA franchises, they (IPL teams) need to do more.

Indian sports journalist
Venkat Ananth

Badenhausen also sees considerable room for growth, although he believes the IPL still has a substantial financial gap to close.

"Its revenue is a fraction of top four American sports leagues, but its valuations are already on par or ahead of the lowest ranked MLB, NHL teams. The IPL has a massive opportunity ahead that could see it continue to close the gap with top American leagues in the decades ahead."

That distinction between revenue and valuation is important.

While the IPL's franchises are already attracting prices comparable to established American sports teams, their underlying businesses still generate considerably less revenue than the biggest US leagues.

The opportunity, therefore, is not simply to sell more broadcasting rights or attract wealthier owners.

It is to turn cricket's enormous audience into a far bigger and sustainable commercial business.

headline: CFTC sues Louisiana after court halts Kalshi, Robinhood and Coinbase event contracts
html_content:
The fight between US states and prediction markets has pulled in some of the best-known names in retail trading, after Louisiana won a court order shutting event contracts out of the state and Washington’s derivatives regulator went to court to stop it.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) said on Friday, 13 November, that it had filed a lawsuit against Louisiana to block the state from prohibiting event contracts offered by CFTC-regulated exchanges, futures commission merchants and clearing houses.

The complaint, brought jointly with the US Justice Department, was filed in the US District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana.

“Event contracts have traded openly in Louisiana for years, in compliance with the Commodity Exchange Act and CFTC regulations,” CFTC chairman Michael Selig said.

He called the state’s “eleventh-hour ‘emergency’ lawsuit” an attempt “to shut down the entire prediction market industry”, adding that the Commission wanted “to maintain the status quo while the federal courts decide this issue in an orderly manner”.

The CFTC said Louisiana is the 12th state it has sued to defend what it describes as its exclusive jurisdiction over derivatives markets.

What the Louisiana order does

Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill, sued the operators in state court on Thursday, 12 November, arguing that event contracts are wagers that need a state gaming licence. Hours later, Judge Jeffrey Johnson of the 21st Judicial District Court in Tangipahoa Parish signed a temporary restraining order. It was granted ex parte, without the companies being heard.

According to the CFTC’s complaint, the order bars defendants from “operating, offering, listing, accepting, clearing, settling, brokering, making a market in, or otherwise facilitating or offering any ‘event contract’” to anyone in Louisiana without a state licence. It covers contracts tied to sports, elections and awards. Legal Sports Report, which reviewed the order, said it also requires operators to geofence the state.

“It’s not complicated: if you aren’t a licensed gaming operator, you aren’t legal,” Murrill wrote on X.

Brokers and crypto exchanges in the frame

According to Legal Sports Report, the order names 31 entities tied to 13 brands, including the brokerage and clearing arms of several mainstream platforms.

Alongside Kalshi and Polymarket’s US business, the list includes Robinhood Markets and Robinhood Derivatives; Coinbase Global and Coinbase Financial Markets; Crypto.com operator Foris and its North American Derivatives Exchange; four Gemini entities; ForecastEx, the prediction market run by Interactive Brokers; and IG Group Holdings, the London-listed owner of US broker tastytrade.

Readers can find more on how two of those platforms work in our Robinhood review and Coinbase review.

The federal case

The federal government argues that event contracts are swaps under the Commodity Exchange Act, so state gambling laws are pre-empted where those contracts trade on CFTC-regulated markets.

It is asking the court for a declaratory judgment and an injunction barring Louisiana from enforcing state law against those markets, including by seeking to extend the Tangipahoa order.

What happens next

The state order lasts 10 days unless extended, and a hearing on Louisiana’s request for a preliminary injunction is scheduled for 30 November.

The case adds to growing state pressure on the sector. More than a dozen states have taken legal action against Kalshi, Polymarket and other prediction market companies, according to The Times-Picayune | The New Orleans Advocate, and Utah filed criminal charges against Kalshi and its co-founders in October.

For US brokers that have added event contracts to their apps, the immediate question is whether a state can switch off a federally regulated product overnight. A federal judge in Louisiana may now be the first to answer it for this state.

headline: Why are Samsung, SK Hynix stocks falling sharply ahead of Nvidia earnings?
html_content:
South Korean chip stocks came under renewed pressure on Monday ahead of Nvidia’s earnings amid concern about artificial intelligence spending.

SK Hynix fell 2.4% in early trading, while Samsung Electronics plunged nearly 3%. The benchmark KOSPI slipped 2.4% to 5,163.18 after opening higher.

The cautious start followed Friday’s technology sell-off on Wall Street, where Nvidia dropped 2.01%, Advanced Micro Devices lost 8.75% and Broadcom declined 4.76%.

That followed a 0.98% KOSPI decline on Friday, when an early rally faded as foreign investors sold shares.

Such reversals suggest traders are demanding stronger evidence that AI investment can sustain its recent pace in the coming years.

Nvidia earnings put AI demand under scrutiny

Nvidia is due to publish fiscal third-quarter results on Tuesday, 17 November, at approximately 4:20 pm Eastern Time, followed by a conference call at 5 pm.

Analysts expect revenue of roughly $109 billion, making the company's forecasts for future sales and profit margins important.

Nvidia buys advanced high-bandwidth memory for its AI accelerators, linking its investment cycle closely to Samsung and SK Hynix. Any indication that customers are delaying data-centre projects could therefore unsettle Korean suppliers.

The results also arrive just days after Huang stepped down on 12 November. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is now serving as interim chief executive, adding questions about leadership continuity to an already demanding earnings test.

Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at Capital.com, told Business Insider on Friday that “AI as a whole continues to be driven by future expectations of monetization, not much should change there.”

Samsung, SK Hynix stocks: Record profits fail to reassure investors

The selling pressure contrasts sharply with the manufacturers’ latest financial results.

Samsung reported third-quarter revenue of 195.3 trillion won and operating profit of 107.4 trillion won, while SK Hynix posted revenue of 104.62 trillion won and operating profit of 83.33 trillion won.

Both benefited from strong demand for memory used in AI servers and other computing infrastructure.

Yet shares weakened on Friday. Samsung closed down 0.96% at 206,000 won, while SK Hynix lost 3.03% to 1.216 million won. Foreign investors sold a net 550.5 billion won of South Korean shares.

“Without prominent negative factors, rising AI uncertainties weighed heavily on the market,” Lee Kyoung-min of Daishin Securities told Yonhap on Friday.

SK Hynix is especially exposed to demand for premium AI memory, whereas Samsung has a broader business spanning semiconductors, smartphones and other consumer products.

Higher borrowing costs and uncertainty about the pace of new data-centre construction are now threatening to overshadow exceptional current earnings.

Analysts disagree over how long the boom can last

The biggest disagreement concerns profits beyond next year, rather than immediate chip orders.

Morgan Stanley recently cut its price targets to 1.6 million won for SK Hynix and 309,000 won for Samsung. Nomura maintained much higher targets of 4.7 million won and 670,000 won.

“The most important debate in the memory market right now is whether we can avoid a ‘cliff in earnings’ in 2028,” Morgan Stanley analyst Shawn Kim warned while speaking with The Korea Herald.

Morgan Stanley expects increased supply and delayed data-centre construction to weigh on longer-term margins. Nomura remains more optimistic about sustained shortages.

headline: Crypto crash: Reasons Bitcoin, altcoins are falling as the Fear and Greed Index sinks
html_content:
The crypto crash continued during the weekend, with Bitcoin and most altcoins plunging to their lowest levels in months. In total, the crypto market has shed over $750 billion in assets since September as the valuation of all tokens has slumped to $2.1 trillion. This article highlights some of the top reasons why cryptocurrencies are falling.

Crypto Fear and Greed Index points to rising fear

Bitcoin and other altcoins are falling this month as investors remain fearful about the industry. The best way to look at this is the Crypto Fear and Greed Index, which has been in a strong sell-off. It dropped to the extreme fear zone of 12 during the weekend, its lowest level in months.

This gauge is modelled in the same approach as the CNN Money Fear and Greed Index that focuses on the stock market. The only difference is that it looks at numbers that are specific to the crypto industry like Bitcoin’s price action, activity in the derivatives market, and social media activity.

The index continues falling, which often leads to panic selling among investors. On the positive side, cryptocurrency rallies often start whenever the index is in the extreme fear zone. Also, most bear markets normally start whenever the index moves to the greed zone.

US bond yields are rising as investors bet on Fed rate hikes

The crypto crash is also happening because of the rising US bond yields. Data shows that the benchmark 10-year has jumped and crossed the 5% metric this month, and the rally may accelerate. 

US bond yields have jumped after a series of US macro data. For example, data showed that the economy expanded by 3.4% in the third quarter, helped by the ongoing data center build up in the US. 

Another data showed that the economy created over 165k jobs last month as the unemployment rate dropped to 4.1%. Also, US inflation has remained steady in the past five years, a trend that has been exacerbated by the ongoing US-Iran war. As a result, the debate among market participants is whether the Fed will hike rates by 0.25% or 0.50% in December.

Soaring ETF outflows and liquidatons

The crypto market crash is also happening as Bitcoin and altcoin ETF outflows continued. The most recent data shows that spot Bitcoin ETFs have shed over $1 billion in assets this month. Also, spot Ethereum and XRP ETFs have continued their outflows, a sign that America’s retail and institutional investors expect the price to drop. 

At the same time, many bullish positions have been liquidated in the past few months. In total, positions worth over $3 billion have been liquidated in the past week. In most cases, these liquidations normally lead to more sell-off of cryptocurrencies. 

Further, the crypto market is also falling as investors abandon risky assets. Indeed, the stock market is also not doing well, with the Dow Jones, Nasdaq 100, and S&P 500 falling by over 3% from their peak. Even the top names, including Nvidia and Micron have all moved into a deep bear market. 

Bitcoin price technicals have contributed to the crypto crash

BTC price chart | Source: TradingView

Technicals have also contributed to the ongoing crypto crash. The daily chart shows that Bitcoin formed a double-top pattern at $87,200, marking the start of its bear market. It has now continued falling, and most recently, it is about to form a death cross pattern. This pattern forms when the 50-day moving average drops below the 200-day EMA. 

The coin has also slumped below the 61.8% Fibonacci Retracement level. Therefore, there is a risk that it will continue falling, which will lead to more downside in the crypto industry.

headline: Gold prices fall below critical levels as Fed rate-hike fears deepen: what’s next?
html_content:
Gold prices fell below $3,900 an ounce on Monday, extending a sharp sell-off as persistent US inflation and growing expectations of another Federal Reserve interest-rate increase overshadowed demand for safe-haven assets.

Spot gold fell 0.4% to $3,868.88 an ounce, while gold futures declined 0.3% to $3,871.92. The US Dollar Index stood at 103.44.

Bullion lost about 4.5% last week and touched its lowest level in more than a year.

Even renewed tensions in the Middle East have failed to produce a sustained recovery, leaving traders focused on whether prices can hold above $3,850.

The latest fall followed Friday's rebound, when a softer monthly producer inflation reading provided temporary relief but failed to reverse broader concerns about monetary policy.

Why geopolitical risks are not lifting gold price

Gold's latest retreat reflects a difficult combination of higher Treasury yields, a stronger dollar and concerns that US interest rates will remain elevated.

Rising yields make interest-bearing assets more attractive relative to gold, which pays no income. A firmer dollar also increases the metal's cost for buyers using other currencies.

Friday's inflation figures offered little relief. The US Producer Price Index rose 0.3% in October, below economists' 0.4% forecast, but annual producer inflation accelerated to 6.5%, its highest since November 2022.

Middle East tensions present another complication. Threats to energy supplies can encourage safe-haven buying, but rising oil prices also risk keeping inflation elevated and forcing the Fed to tighten policy.

Independent metals analyst Tai Wong captured that tension on Friday, telling Reuters: "It's been a tough week for gold, which may struggle to retake 4,000 with Fed hawks out in force."

Gold price today: December rate expectations put Fed in control

Markets increasingly believe US policymakers will raise borrowing costs again next month.

CME FedWatch probabilities cited in Monday's market reports showed a 94% chance of a quarter-point December increase and a 6% probability of a larger half-point move.

Those figures reflect traders' expectations, not a central bank decision. More importantly for gold, investors are beginning to weigh whether tightening could continue into 2027.

Kansas City Fed President Jeff Schmid warned on Sunday that inflation remained too high, while other policymakers have expressed concern about persistent price pressures.

Attention now turns to Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who is scheduled to deliver opening remarks at a productivity conference on Monday at noon Eastern Time.

His remarks are billed as an introduction to a conference, not a policy speech.

The minutes of the Fed's October policy meeting follow on Wednesday at 2 pm Eastern. Any suggestion that officials favour further increases could reinforce upward pressure on yields and the dollar.

Can gold price defend $3,850 or slide towards $3,800?

Gold's failure to maintain the $4,000 threshold has weakened its near-term technical picture.

Around $3,850 is the first level to watch after last week's slide. A decisive break could expose $3,800, identified by analysts as a potential downside target.

Ole Hansen, Saxo Bank's head of commodity strategy, told Kitco that losing $4,000 had damaged gold's outlook. Still, he noted that “central banks continue accumulating bullion,” while exchange-traded fund demand could cushion the correction.

That distinction matters because gold can retain appeal as a reserve asset even while higher real yields encourage investors to reduce short-term exposure.

Eren Sengezer warned in an FXStreet forecast that “additional USD gains and a leg higher in US T-bond yields” could follow if Fed officials indicated larger or consecutive rate increases.

headline: Bitcoin price faces a $60,000 test: is a deeper crash coming?
html_content:
Bitcoin (BTC) remained under pressure on Monday, trading around $64,500 after extending its decline to $62,006 last week, a level not seen since mid-July.

The cryptocurrency has now recorded six consecutive weekly losses, shedding more than 24% of its value since early October as persistent institutional selling and weakening investor confidence weigh on the market.

US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) have also experienced substantial withdrawals, recording more than $2.3 billion in combined net outflows over the past two weeks.

Bitcoin ETFs record $2.35 billion in outflows as institutional demand weakens

Institutional demand for Bitcoin continued to deteriorate last week as US spot ETFs recorded another substantial round of withdrawals.

According to SoSoValue, the investment products experienced $1.07 billion in net outflows last week, following $1.28 billion in withdrawals the previous week.

The combined $2.35 billion in outflows represents two consecutive weeks of billion-dollar withdrawals.

The continued withdrawals suggest that institutional investors are reducing their exposure to Bitcoin amid deteriorating market conditions.

If the negative flow trend continues this week, Bitcoin could face additional pressure as investors reassess their exposure to risk-sensitive assets.

Bitcoin's latest sell-off has also triggered a substantial reduction in leveraged market exposure.

According to analysts, the weekend downturn eliminated almost all leveraged positions established since the August rally.

The market sentiment and momentum indicators have deteriorated to some of their weakest readings in years.

This suggests that the recent correction has been particularly severe, forcing traders to unwind positions as prices continued falling.

However, Bitcoin's deeply stretched indicators could support a short-term relief rally. Despite that, a sustained recovery remains uncertain because large Bitcoin holders continue to sell.

In an email to Invezz, Nick Forster, founder and CEO of Derive.XYZ, stated that Bitcoin's sharp rebound from Sunday's low shows buyers are still willing to step in.

Expert View

The immediate question is whether Bitcoin can hold its recovery above $60K or whether another wave of selling pushes prices towards the July low of $57.7K. Markets are also closely watching US interest rate expectations following another elevated inflation reading, with the Federal Reserve's December meeting approaching.

Founder and CEO of Derive.XYZ
Nick Forster

Bitcoin price forecast: BTC breaks below 200-week SMA and key Fibonacci support

Bitcoin's weekly technical structure has weakened considerably following six consecutive weeks of losses.

The cryptocurrency has declined more than 24% since early October, breaking below several important technical levels.

Last week, BTC closed the weekly candle below its 200-week Simple Moving Average (SMA), currently at $68,194.

The 200-week SMA is widely monitored as a long-term trend indicator and has historically attracted attention during major Bitcoin market corrections.

A sustained move below this level suggests that the broader technical outlook has deteriorated. Bitcoin also closed below the 78.6% Fibonacci retracement level at $65,616.

This level is derived from the August 2024 low near $49,000 and the October 2025 record high of $126,199.

The breakdown below both technical barriers reinforces the bearish outlook and suggests that sellers remain in control.

At the time of writing, BTC trades around $64,500, remaining below the Fibonacci level. If selling pressure continues, Bitcoin could extend its decline toward the psychological $60,000 support level.

Momentum indicators on the weekly chart also support the bearish outlook. The Relative Strength Index (RSI) stands around 37, below the neutral 50 level, suggesting that sellers retain an advantage.

Meanwhile, the Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD) histogram registered a bearish crossover last week, which remains intact.

This indicates that downside momentum continues to dominate the longer-term trend.

However, a recovery above the $65,616 Fibonacci level could allow Bitcoin to challenge the 200-week SMA near $68,194.

Reclaiming these levels would improve the technical structure, although additional confirmation would be needed to establish a sustained bullish reversal.

Bitcoin's daily chart also reflects persistent selling pressure, although momentum indicators suggest that the decline may be becoming overstretched.

BTC remains significantly below its major daily Exponential Moving Averages (EMAs). The 200-day EMA stands around $75,946, while the 100-day EMA is positioned near $76,470.

The 50-day EMA sits slightly higher at $76,701. These moving averages form a concentrated resistance zone between approximately $75,946 and $76,701.

Trading well below this cluster suggests that Bitcoin's short- and medium-term trends remain bearish.

Bitcoin's next major move will likely depend on whether buyers can defend recent lows and reclaim previously broken technical levels.

The immediate downside reference is last week's low near $62,006. A sustained breakdown below this level could increase selling pressure and expose Bitcoin to the psychological $60,000 mark.

On the upside, the first important level to reclaim is the 78.6% Fibonacci retracement at $65,616. A sustained recovery above this barrier could encourage buyers to target the 200-week SMA around $68,194.

Reclaiming the 200-week average would provide an early indication that Bitcoin's longer-term technical structure is improving.

However, a stronger recovery would still face resistance from the daily EMA cluster between $75,946 and $76,701.

A decisive breakout above this region would suggest that bearish momentum is weakening and could open the door to a recovery toward the $85,000 horizontal resistance.

headline: Nvidia stock faces a new Jensen Huang crisis as Elon Musk enters the fight
html_content:
Elon Musk has joined a campaign calling for Jensen Huang to return as Nvidia chief executive, adding pressure on the chipmaker's board days after his abrupt resignation.

An open letter had attracted more than 158,000 signatures by late Sunday. More than 7,500 signatories identified themselves as Nvidia employees, although those affiliations have not been independently verified.

The campaign comes as Nvidia prepares to report quarterly earnings on Tuesday. Its shares closed Friday at $162.85, down 2.01%, after falling 4.34% the previous session.

Elon Musk joins campaign to bring Jensen Huang back

Musk said on Friday that he would sign the petition seeking Huang's reinstatement. Other supporters include Epic Games chief Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator president Garry Tan.

The letter asks Nvidia's directors to reinstate Huang while an independent investigation establishes the facts. It also seeks a fair hearing and a public explanation of the board's decision.

The campaign has grown beyond employee frustration. Investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker have urged directors to keep their options open, while the Financial Times reported on Sunday that Huang had discussed a possible return with confidants.

One ally was organising Silicon Valley executives to lobby the board and potentially seek White House support, according to the newspaper.

Huang's importance extends well beyond Nvidia's leadership structure. He spent 33 years building the company into a central supplier of chips powering the AI boom.

Technology analyst Dan Ives described his departure as "a gut punch to the industry" in comments to CBS News.

Nvidia board faces pressure from Washington

Any decision to reinstate Huang would face political and governance questions.

Huang resigned following reports concerning personal relationships, including one involving a woman suspected of links to Chinese intelligence.

Those suspicions remain allegations, while questions about Nvidia's compliance with US chip-export controls have prompted scrutiny in Washington.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that Nvidia should appoint an outsider and called for a major leadership overhaul. He also requested answers within 10 days about the company's export-control compliance.

Such scrutiny could also complicate relationships with government customers and intensify worries over future chip sales abroad.

The Financial Times previously reported that Nvidia's board had approached Arm chief executive Rene Haas about the role. Nvidia has not announced a permanent successor.

For now, chief financial officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO.

Gil Luria of DA Davidson told Reuters that Kress was "well respected by investors" and capable of steering Nvidia through a difficult period.

The board must therefore balance demands for Huang's return against the need to reassure regulators and shareholders that its governance is credible.

What Tuesday's earnings mean for Nvidia stock

Nvidia's shares are roughly 32% below their October peak of $239.24, reflecting concerns that extend beyond succession.

The company previously projected fiscal third-quarter revenue of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, with gross margins around 74%. Results are due Tuesday at approximately 4:20 pm Eastern, followed by a conference call at 5 pm.

Investors will examine data-centre sales, future guidance and whether customers remain committed to major AI infrastructure projects.

Daniela Hathorn of Capital.com told Business Insider that AI investment "continues to be driven by future expectations of monetization," suggesting Huang's departure need not derail the broader industry's prospects.

Strong earnings and a credible succession plan could help restore confidence. Disappointing forecasts or prolonged boardroom conflict could deepen the sell-off.

The letter asks Nvidia's directors to reinstate Huang while an independent investigation establishes the facts. It also seeks a fair hearing and a public explanation of the board's decision. The campaign has grown beyond employee frustration. Investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker have urged directors to keep their options open, while the Financial Times reported on Sunday that Huang had discussed a possible return with confidants. One ally was organising Silicon Valley executives to lobby the board and potentially seek White House support, according to the newspaper. Huang's importance extends well beyond Nvidia's leadership structure. He spent 33 years building the company into a central supplier of chips powering the AI boom. Technology analyst Dan Ives described his departure as "a gut punch to the industry" in comments to CBS News. Huang resigned following reports concerning personal relationships, including one involving a woman suspected of links to Chinese intelligence. Those suspicions remain allegations, while questions about Nvidia's compliance with US chip-export controls have prompted scrutiny in Washington. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that Nvidia should appoint an outsider and called for a major leadership overhaul. Such scrutiny could also complicate relationships with government customers and intensify worries over future chip sales abroad. Gil Luria of DA Davidson told Reuters that Kress was "well respected by investors" and capable of steering Nvidia through a difficult period. The board must therefore balance demands for Huang's return against the need to reassure regulators and shareholders that its governance is credible. Investors will examine data-centre sales, future guidance and whether customers remain committed to major AI infrastructure projects. headline: Oil prices near $95: will Brent crude crash below $90 as supply glut grows?
html_content:
Oil prices fell on Monday as growing expectations of a global supply surplus outweighed continuing security risks in the Middle East, raising questions about whether Brent crude could retreat below $90 a barrel.

Brent futures slipped 0.6% to $95.30 a barrel at 04:27 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude declined 0.3% to $88.34.

The decline followed a reversal in supply expectations. After months of disruption from the conflict involving Iran, the International Energy Agency now expects the world oil market to move into surplus before the year ends.

Oil price today: Supply rebounds as demand weakens

The IEA's November report marked a major reversal in expectations, projecting that global oil supply will exceed demand by 1.7 million barrels a day in the fourth quarter.

World production rose by 2.3 million barrels a day in October to 105.4 million as Gulf shipments recovered, even as attacks on energy infrastructure continued.

Meanwhile, observed inventories increased by 52 million barrels during October, their first monthly rise since June. The agency expects global oil demand to fall by 2.7 million barrels a day across 2026.

China has added to the bearish picture. Its refinery throughput fell 8.1% from a year earlier in October, suggesting softer crude requirements from one of the world's largest consumers.

Tim Waterer, chief analyst at KCM Trade, told Reuters that the prospect of excess supply was replacing fears of shortages among traders.

“That shift in narrative is clearly dampening the tone,” he said.

The United States has also extended a waiver of shipping restrictions, giving fuel suppliers more flexibility to move cargoes between domestic ports.

Brent crude forecast: Middle East risks could prevent a collapse

Falling prices do not mean the disruption around the Strait of Hormuz has ended.

Although exports have recovered, shipping remains expensive and vulnerable to renewed attacks. The IEA said Gulf exports excluding Oman reached 18.4 million barrels daily in October, still 26% below pre-war levels, highlighting the fragility of that recovery despite recent progress.

Iranian state media reported on Sunday that a tanker struck a naval mine, an account that could not be independently confirmed.

The IEA also cautioned that observed global oil inventories were still 462 million barrels below their level at the start of the conflict. Diesel supplies remain particularly constrained, despite easing crude-market conditions.

That leaves room for a renewed price rally if shipments are interrupted again.

BCA Research, in commentary reported by Investing.com, warned: “Investors should not treat a rapid resolution to the conflict as a foregone conclusion.”

The firm expects Brent to trade between $90 and $110 a barrel, arguing that much of the geopolitical risk premium has already disappeared.

Its assessment suggests a ceasefire might produce only limited additional downside, whereas another serious disruption could bring sharp gains.

Will Brent crude break below $90?

Near-term forecasts remain cautious. Ajit Mishra, senior vice-president of research at Religare Broking, told Moneycontrol:

“Brent crude oil could potentially test $90-92 per barrel in overseas trade, with prices likely to remain volatile with a downward bias.”

Technical analysis published last week identified support between $93.25 and $95.25. A sustained weekly break could expose the $89-$90 range, followed by $85-$86.

Conversely, a recovery above $100-$101 would challenge the view that the latest decline has further to run.

headline: Will Solana price crash below $60 as ETF outflows hit six-week streak?
html_content:
Solana (SOL) is back in the green after a bearish weekend, with the cryptocurrency now trading at $71 after falling to $67, its lowest level since late June.

The cryptocurrency continues to struggle as institutional demand weakens, with US spot Solana exchange-traded funds (ETFs) recording their sixth consecutive week of net withdrawals.

The continued withdrawals have coincided with a broader deterioration in Solana's technical outlook. SOL remains significantly below its major moving averages and a previously supportive ascending trendline.

Solana ETFs record six consecutive weeks of outflows

Institutional demand for Solana has continued to weaken, with spot ETFs experiencing persistent withdrawals since October.

According to SoSoValue, US spot Solana ETFs recorded $32.05 million in net outflows last week.

The withdrawals marked the sixth consecutive week of negative net flows, suggesting a sustained reduction in investor exposure through regulated investment products.

If the outflow trend persists this week, it could contribute to additional selling pressure and make it more difficult for SOL to establish a sustained recovery.

A sustained return to positive ETF inflows would provide stronger evidence that institutional confidence is beginning to improve. Until then, Solana's recovery could remain vulnerable to renewed selling.

Solana falls to a four-month low as bearish trend persists

Solana's latest decline pushed its price to $67.41, its lowest level in approximately four months.

Although SOL subsequently recovered to around $71.02 on Monday, the rebound has done little to change its broader bearish technical structure.

Solana continues to trade well below its major daily Exponential Moving Averages. The 50-day EMA stands near $94.62, while the 100-day EMA is positioned around $95.80.

Meanwhile, the 200-day EMA sits at approximately $96.14. These moving averages form a concentrated resistance zone that could limit recovery attempts.

Solana has also broken below a previously supportive ascending trendline, which now acts as resistance around $91.06.

The breakdown indicates that the cryptocurrency has lost an important technical structure that previously supported higher prices.

Despite the prevailing bearish outlook, Solana's momentum indicators suggest that the recent decline may be becoming overstretched.

The daily Relative Strength Index (RSI) stands near 20, placing SOL deep in oversold territory.

An RSI reading below 30 generally indicates that selling pressure has become excessive relative to recent price movements.

Meanwhile, Solana's Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD) indicator remains in negative territory.

The negative MACD reading suggests that bearish momentum continues to dominate despite the possibility of a short-term rebound.

The combination of deeply oversold RSI conditions and negative MACD readings presents a mixed near-term outlook.

While a temporary recovery is possible, the broader technical structure remains bearish. A successful defense of $67.41 could encourage buyers to establish positions and potentially support a period of consolidation.

However, a sustained breakdown below the recent low would weaken the technical outlook further.

The absence of clear technical support below $67.41 increases uncertainty about where buyers might return.

On the upside, Solana faces immediate resistance at $78.35. A sustained move above this horizontal resistance would suggest that buyers are regaining some short-term control.

However, SOL would still need to overcome the former ascending trendline near $91.06. Reclaiming this level would represent a more meaningful technical improvement, potentially signaling that the recent breakdown is losing momentum.

Beyond $91.06, Solana faces a dense resistance cluster formed by its major daily EMAs. The 50-day EMA stands at $94.62, followed by the 100-day EMA at $95.80 and the 200-day EMA at $96.14.

A breakout above this zone could encourage buyers to target the horizontal resistance near $97.77.

headline: Column: What trustworthy AI investing should look like
html_content:
AI is no longer just in the background; it is reading market data, writing research and increasingly nudging people towards buying and selling.

Research for the FCA’s Mills Review found that around 26% of adults trust tools such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini for financial advice, yet only 40% know there is no formal route to recourse if that advice goes wrong.

The stakes rise as these tools start to act, not just advise.

As the Mills Review puts it, “As AI moves from recommending to acting, and firms and consumers delegate more, risks shift from harm within a single firm towards system-wide harms.” So the question is not whether investors will use AI, but how they can tell which AI deserves their trust.

My answer is simple. Investment intelligence must be judged by the consistency of the insights it produces, by how responsibly they are generated and communicated, and ultimately by whether an organisation takes responsibility for its output.

Not all AI is the same

Before you get to trust, you have to have the right tools for the job. LLMs are excellent at reading news, summarising filings and screening sentiment, but there is academic evidence that they are poor at stock selection: what to buy, when to buy, when to sell and what to replace it with. You don’t ask a dentist to perform brain surgery, so don’t ask a chatbot for stock tips when the model was never trained for it and to make matters worse, it is likely to sound plausible.

Prediction needs domain-specific systems. At InvestorAi, we built neural networks that read prices, volumes, fundamentals and corporate events as images, recognising patterns in noisy, incomplete data. This is also different from algo trading, which follows pre-written rules which can be copied. In AI investing, the AI does the research, finds opportunities and builds portfolios by finding its own patterns in the data.

My preferred architecture uses specialist predictive models for stock picking and portfolio construction, an LLM for news and sentiment screening and agents to orchestrate execution within very clear guardrails.

Judge the process, not just the prediction

A good call can be luck, but getting it right on a consistent basis matters more. It’s the difference between betting blind on the Grand National and running masses of data through domain-specific trained models to pick a runner. Neither is guaranteed to win, but I know which one I would side with. How does this translate to investing with AI?

  • A track record you can inspect. Unlike a chatbot's answer, a live model leaves a record. Ours has picked stocks for real investors in India, under regulatory oversight, since April 2021. It won't get everything right, but you can see exactly what it has done. Look for consistency and repeatable performance over time rather than one standout year. 
  • Disciplined testing. Treat back-tested results with caution and in the absence of a live track record, make sure models were tested against data they had never seen. In our own research, hold-out data is sealed and opened exactly once, and every failure is logged. Rules like these stop a model from being tuned until it merely looks good on paper.
  • Honesty about uncertainty. A trustworthy system says when it isn't confident. Our models use conviction gating: they act only when their confidence clears a learned threshold; otherwise they stay out.

Accountability cannot be outsourced

Technology changes how advice is produced, not who is responsible for it. Regulators in different markets are reaching the same conclusion. In the UK, the Treasury reports strong industry support for the FCA's “tech-neutral, outcomes-focused approach”.  The Chairman of SEBI (India’s securities regulator), Tuhin Kanta Pandey, is quoted as saying, “Technology cannot dilute accountability”. It’s impossible to disagree.

That responsibility cannot be passed to a model, or to an insurer. Disclaiming “model behaviour” is not good enough; providers must own outputs, not just intent. Human oversight, clear processes and ownership of outcomes are a far better guide to how responsibly an organisation deploys AI. Human-in-the-loop needs to be more than a box-ticking exercise, and for us, every AI-picked strategy we offer runs with expert oversight. As Mills notes, “Oversight can also weaken if reviewers are overloaded, lack the right information or rely too readily on model outputs.” 

As AI moves from recommending to acting, guardrails matter as much as models. Agents need kill switches, position limits and the ability for a human to override them at any point. Ultimately, regulation sets a floor. AI is moving faster than any regulator can write rules, so it falls to the industry to go beyond that floor rather than wait for it to catch up.

Intelligence, with accountability

AI can close information gaps that have long disadvantaged ordinary investors. In the UK, only around 9% of adults use traditional financial advice, and it’s lower in India. Because AI’s marginal cost falls with scale, good investment research no longer has to be a privilege of the few. That is what AI is for.

That promise holds only if the intelligence is earned: the right model for the job, tested honestly, explained clearly, and with a regulated party answering for the outcome. Trustworthy AI investing is not the AI that sounds most confident. It is the AI that can demonstrate consistency, with someone standing behind it.

(Bruce Keith is the CEO and Cofounder of InvestorAi. He is based in Mumbai and London and the views are his own)
